title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
You know the feeling. It's 2 p.m. on a Tuesday. You've been "working" for four hours, but when you try to name one thing you actually finished, your mind goes blank. Your browser has nineteen tabs open. Your phone has buzzed forty times. You answered three emails, started two documents, skimmed a report, and replied to a message you should have ignored. You were busy all morning. You were also, in any meaningful sense, not working at all.

Here is the uncomfortable truth this book is built on: you are not bad at focusing. You are living in a world engineered to make focus nearly impossible. Every app on your phone, every notification, every infinite scroll was designed by teams of brilliant people whose job is to pull your attention away from whatever you're doing and hold it hostage. You are bringing a human brain to a fight against billion-dollar attention machines. Of course you're losing.

But you don't have to keep losing. The way out is not another productivity app or a more elaborate to-do list. The way out is a single, almost old-fashioned practice: doing one thing at a time.

Single-tasking sounds too simple to matter. It isn't. When you switch tasks, your brain doesn't glide from one to the next; it lurches. Part of your mind stays stuck on the email you just left while you try to write the report. Researchers call this attention residue, and it means every "quick check" costs you minutes of real focus afterward. Do that twenty times a day and you've quietly destroyed hours. Multitasking isn't doing two things at once. It's doing two things badly, in rapid alternation, while feeling exhausted.

So here is what single-tasking actually looks like in practice.

First, decide before you start. Not "work on the project" but "draft the introduction to the project." Vague intentions invite distraction; specific ones resist it. Write the one thing down where you can see it.

Second, make distraction hard, not just discouraged. Willpower is a terrible strategy. Put your phone in another room, not face-down on your desk. Close every tab you don't need. If you can't resist checking something, use a blocker. Design your environment so that focusing is the path of least resistance, because your brain will always take that path.

Third, work in honest blocks. Twenty-five minutes or fifty, whatever fits your life, but during that block you do the one thing. When the urge to check something arrives, and it will, notice it and let it pass. The urge is not a command. It's a habit waving at you. You can wave back and keep working.

Fourth, protect your transitions. Between blocks, take a real break. Stand up. Look out a window. Don't fill every gap with a screen. The point of rest is to let your attention reset, not to flood it with more input.

You will not do this perfectly. Some days the notifications win. That's fine. The goal is not monastic purity; it's a shift in the ratio. A few genuinely focused hours will outperform a whole distracted day, every time.

The world will keep buzzing. Your job is not to silence it entirely. Your job is to decide, again and again, what deserves your attention right now, and then to give it fully. One thing. Then the next. That's the whole method. Start today, with whatever is in front of you.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
People always ask me the same question when they find out I started my first business with $87 and a laptop that overheated if you looked at it wrong. They lean in, expecting some secret. A grant. An investor. A rich uncle. And I love watching their faces fall when I say, "Nope. I just refused to spend money I didn't have."

Here's the thing nobody tells you: money is the least creative resource you have. When you've got cash, you solve problems by writing checks. When you don't, you solve problems by actually thinking. Poverty, it turns out, is a fantastic brainstorming tool.

I once ran an entire marketing campaign from the self-checkout line at a grocery store. True story. I couldn't afford Facebook ads, so I printed my website on the back of my business cards and handed them out at a farmers market like I was passing out flyers for a lost dog. It felt pathetic. It worked. Three of those people are still customers eight years later.

So let me save you some tuition money. Here's what I wish someone had told me before I maxed out a credit card on "branding."

1. Sell before you build. I spent six weeks designing a logo for a business that had zero customers. Zero. Meanwhile, a friend of mine sold her first forty orders of homemade granola before she owned a single bag or a label. She took orders in a Google Form and delivered them in Ziploc bags with a Sharpie label. Nobody cared. They cared about the granola. Build the thing people pay for, not the thing that looks nice on Instagram.

2. Your first office is wherever you already are. My first "headquarters" was a corner of my kitchen table, and my "boardroom" was the parking lot of a Panera. I'd take calls in my car and pretend there was traffic so I could finish a thought. You do not need a coworking membership. You need a phone and the audacity to answer it.

3. Barter like your life depends on it. Early on, I traded website design for dental work. I'm not kidding. My teeth have never looked better and my site still converts. Small business is a community of people who are all a little broke and a lot resourceful. Ask for what you need and offer what you've got. The worst that happens is someone says no and you move on with your day.

4. Free tools are embarrassingly good now. When I started, "free software" meant a spreadsheet with a virus. Today you can run an entire company on free tiers—email, invoicing, project management, design. I once built a customer database out of a free survey tool because I didn't want to pay for a CRM. Was it elegant? No. Did it work? For two years. Spend your money on things that make money, and use free stuff for everything else.

The real secret, though, isn't a tactic. It's a mindset shift that took me way too long to learn: being broke forces you to be close to your customer. You can't afford to guess. You can't afford to be fancy. You have to talk to people, ask them what they want, and hand them something useful before you've polished the edges.

My first sale was $12. I remember it because I did a little dance in my kitchen and my dog barked at me. That $12 felt better than any check I've cashed since. Not because of the money—because it proved the idea was real. And you don't need a bank account to prove an idea is real. You need a customer, a little nerve, and the willingness to look a bit scrappy while you figure it out.

So stop waiting for the funding. Start with the $87. Or the $8. The number doesn't matter. The starting does.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
The first office we ever had was above a nail salon, and I mean directly above it. Every morning at 9 a.m. the smell of acrylic and acetone would drift up through the floorboards and settle into our keyboards, and by noon the whole place smelled like a chemistry experiment gone wrong. We told investors it was "a vibrant startup space." We told ourselves it built character. Mostly we just got headaches.

There were six of us in those days, and none of us really knew what we were doing. I had dropped out of a PhD program in computer science, which sounds impressive until you realize I dropped out because I couldn't get my thesis committee to agree on anything, including lunch. Our lead engineer, Dmitri, had spent four years building trading systems on Wall Street before deciding he hated money, or at least hated the people who had it. He wore the same gray hoodie every single day for what I'm pretty sure was eight months. We never confirmed this because none of us wanted to ask, but there was a running office pool about it.

The culture, if you could call it that, was basically whatever kept us from killing each other. We had a rule that anyone could interrupt anyone else at any time, which sounds democratic until you're trying to debug a query parser and someone taps you on the shoulder to ask whether we should buy a second coffee machine. We had another rule that the person who broke the build had to bring in donuts the next morning. This worked great until Dmitri broke the build three days in a row and showed up with three dozen donuts, which he ate mostly himself while staring at us defiantly.

What I remember most clearly is the whiteboard. We had this enormous whiteboard that took up an entire wall, and every Friday we'd write down the dumbest idea anyone had proposed that week and vote on it. The winner got to keep their idea on the board for the following week, no matter how absurd. One week the winning idea was "let users search for things by screaming into their microphone." Another week it was "make the homepage a picture of my cat." For the record, the cat idea actually got implemented as an easter egg, and I still get emails about it from strangers to this day.

We were naive in ways that make me wince now. We thought we could index the entire web with three servers and a borrowed database license. We thought users would read our help documentation. We thought the search results were good, which they absolutely were not. I remember typing a query for "best pizza near me" and getting back a page about pizza history, a link to a domain that had expired in 1997, and a forum post from a guy arguing that pizza was a government conspiracy. We shipped it anyway. We were so proud.

But there was something magic in that room, under the nail salon, with the acetone smell and the gray hoodie and the donuts. We didn't know what we were building, not really. We just knew we wanted to build it together, and that none of us wanted to go back to whatever we'd been doing before. That's the thing nobody tells you about the early days. You don't remember the strategy or the roadmap. You remember the smell of the floor and the sound of someone laughing at a terrible idea at 11 p.m. on a Tuesday. That's the whole memoir, honestly. The rest is just footnotes.

title: career advice book|quitting a stable job to do work you care about
text:
Most people who hate their jobs don’t quit. They negotiate. They get the title bump, the extra week of vacation, the “flexible Fridays” that somehow still require you to be on Slack at 7 p.m. And then they tell themselves the story that keeps them there for another decade: *it’s not that bad.*

It’s not that bad. That’s the phrase. Listen for it. It’s the sound of a life leaking out one quarter at a time.

I’m not going to give you the “follow your passion” speech. Passion is overrated and mostly a marketing term. What I’m talking about is narrower and harder: work you actually care about, the kind that makes you sit up a little straighter when you describe it at a party. If you can’t remember the last time you felt that, keep reading.

Here’s the number that should scare you. The average person spends about 90,000 hours at work over a lifetime. Ninety thousand. If you’re 35 and you’ve been grinding for 12 years, you’ve already burned roughly 25,000 of them. You don’t get a rebate on the ones you spent doing something you didn’t believe in. You don’t get to trade them in.

I quit a job that paid $148,000 a year to do something that paid $52,000 and scared me so much I couldn’t sleep for a week. People thought I was having a breakdown. My father asked me twice if I was sure. I was not sure. I was terrified. But I was more terrified of staying. That’s the test, by the way. Not “am I excited?” Excitement is cheap. The real question is: *am I more afraid of leaving than of staying?* When the answer flips, you’re done. You just haven’t admitted it yet.

Now, the practical part, because I’m not a lunatic. You need runway. Twelve months of expenses in the bank is ideal. Six is workable if you have a spouse with benefits or a side income. Less than six and you’re not making a career decision, you’re making a panic decision, and panic decisions have a way of becoming expensive. Don’t quit on a Friday and “figure it out.” Have a plan for Monday morning. Even a bad plan beats a void.

And for God’s sake, don’t quit to “find yourself.” Find yourself on the weekend. Quit because you’ve found something you want to build, or someone you want to help, or a problem that won’t leave you alone. That’s the only fuel that lasts past month three.

One more thing, and this is the part nobody tells you: the first year will probably be worse than your stable job. Less money, more doubt, and a strange loneliness that comes from no longer having a title to hide behind. My first year I made $31,000 and cried in a parking garage twice. I’m not proud of it. I’m just telling you the truth so you don’t think you’re failing when it happens.

But here’s what I got in exchange. I got to work on things I’d defend in an argument. I got to look at my calendar and recognize my own handwriting in it. I got to stop rehearsing the sentence *it’s not that bad.*

You’ve got one life and a finite number of Mondays. Spend them on something you’d fight for.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Chapter 7: The Iceberg Below the Table

 What They Say vs. What They Need

The most expensive mistake in negotiation is answering the question you were asked instead of solving the problem you were handed.

In 2019, I spent three weeks negotiating what I thought was a straightforward consulting contract with a regional hospital network. Their procurement director, a meticulous man named Dale, opened our first session by saying, "We need you to cut your fee by twenty percent." I did what any trained negotiator would do: I pushed back on the number. We went three rounds on price—I offered eight percent, he countered at fifteen, we landed at eleven. I walked out of that room feeling victorious. I had defended my value.

Two months later, the engagement fell apart. Not because of the fee. Because Dale had never actually cared about the fee. What he cared about—what he had been *told* to care about by his CFO—was that the project show a defensible return on investment within the fiscal year. His board had been burned by consultants before, and Dale's real job in that negotiation was to protect himself from looking foolish in front of the finance committee. The twenty percent was a smokescreen. What he needed was a guarantee, a milestone-based payment structure, and a case study he could present in October. I gave him none of those things, because I never asked.

I learned more from that failure than from any deal I've closed since.

The iceberg principle. In every negotiation, positions float above the waterline: "Cut your fee." "Deliver by March." "We need exclusivity." These are demands, and they're visible, specific, and almost always negotiable. Beneath them sits the mass of the iceberg—interests, anxieties, incentives, and the story the other person will have to tell their boss, their board, or their spouse. You cannot see any of it from across the table. You can only ask.

Ask the question behind the question. When someone states a demand, resist the urge to counter it immediately. Instead, get curious about its origin: *"Help me understand what's driving that number."* Or: *"If we solved that, what would it unlock for you?"* Or the simplest and most disarming version: *"What does a great outcome look like for you six months from now?"* People rarely lie when asked about their future; they simply have never been asked.

Listen for the third thing. In most negotiations, each side states two or three obvious requirements—price, timeline, scope. The real information lives in the casual aside, the sigh before the answer, the topic they keep circling back to. Dale mentioned his finance committee three times in our first meeting. I heard it as small talk. It was the entire negotiation.

Test your read before you commit. Once you think you've found the underlying interest, say it back plainly: *"It sounds like the fee isn't the real issue—it's that you need certainty the investment pays off this year. Is that fair?"* If you're wrong, you've lost nothing and learned something. If you're right, you've just moved the conversation from combat to collaboration. Dale, had I asked, would have told me exactly this. People are usually relieved when someone finally asks.

Remember that interests are not weaknesses. A common fear is that probing for what the other side really wants gives them an advantage. The opposite is true. When you understand someone's interests, you can craft options that cost you little and are worth a great deal to them—payment terms instead of price cuts, phased delivery instead of rushed deadlines. The pie gets bigger precisely because you stopped arguing about the slice.

I eventually got a second chance with that hospital network, a year later. Different project, same Dale. This time, my first question wasn't about fees. It was: "What does the finance committee need to see in October?" We closed in a week—at my full rate—because I finally negotiated with the man in front of me instead of the demand on the table.

The lesson is simple, though not easy: before you argue about what they're asking for, find out what they're afraid of, what they're measured on, and what story they need to tell when the meeting is over. The position is the noise. The interest is the signal. Ask until you hear it.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
The first time I tried to “get in shape,” I wrote a plan that would have made an Olympic coach weep with envy. Six days a week. Ninety minutes a day. A spreadsheet. Color-coded, obviously. I lasted eleven days. On day twelve I ate a family-sized bag of pretzels standing over the sink at 10 p.m. and decided I was simply not a fitness person.

Here’s the thing nobody tells you: I wasn’t a fitness person because my plan required me to become one overnight. I designed a habit for the person I wished I were, not the person who actually lives in my house and forgets where she put her coffee down.

That’s why I now swear by the two-minute rule. If a new habit takes more than two minutes to start, it’s too big. Not too big forever. Too big for right now. “Read before bed” becomes “read one page.” “Start running” becomes “put on your running shoes.” “Eat better” becomes “eat one vegetable with lunch.” It feels almost insultingly easy. That’s the point. You cannot fail at putting on shoes. I have tried. It’s very hard to fail at shoes.

1. Shrink it until it’s laughable. If your habit sounds impressive when you tell someone, it’s probably too big. “I’m going to floss one tooth” is not impressive. It is, however, a thing you will actually do. And here’s the sneaky part: once you’re flossing one tooth, flossing the other thirty-one feels weirdly natural. Starting is the hard part. Make starting embarrassingly easy.

2. Anchor it to something you already do. I brush my teeth every night. I don’t think about it, I don’t motivate myself for it, I just do it. So my tiny habits live right after brushing. One push-up. One page. One sentence in a journal. Existing habits are free real estate, and you should be squatting on all of it.

3. Track it, but keep it stupid. I used to use an elaborate app with charts and streaks and confetti animations. Then I missed a day, the streak died, and I quit for a month out of spite. Now I use a paper calendar and a pen. Done? Draw an X. That’s it. There is no confetti. The lack of confetti has never once made me quit.

I want to be honest with you, because I like you. Some days my habit is genuinely just the two-minute version. One push-up. One page. That’s the whole workout. And I used to feel like a fraud on those days, until I realized that showing up tiny is how you build the identity. You’re not trying to get fit this week. You’re trying to become someone who works out. And someone who works out is just a person who keeps showing up, even when showing up is one push-up.

So pick one habit. Shrink it until it’s almost silly. Attach it to your toothbrush. Draw an X. And when you inevitably have a pretzel-over-the-sink kind of day, don’t throw out the whole plan — just do the two-minute version and move on. Future you, the one who actually works out, will be extremely grateful.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
Here's a chapter written in the style of a bestselling habit book — conversational, personal, with concrete examples.

---

CHAPTER 7: So Small You Can't Fail

Let me tell you about the dumbest workout plan I ever made. I'm talking Olympic-level delusional. Six days a week, ninety minutes a day, cardio plus lifting plus stretching, and — this is the best part — I wrote it out in a color-coded spreadsheet. I was so proud of that spreadsheet. I printed it. I put it on my fridge.

I followed it for four days. Four. Then life happened, and by "life" I mean I was tired, and by "tired" I mean I sat on the couch eating cereal straight from the box while my color-coded spreadsheet judged me from the fridge.

Here's what I learned from that failure, and from about a hundred failures like it: the problem wasn't my discipline. The problem was the size of the plan. I'd designed a habit for the person I wanted to be, not the person I actually was on a Tuesday at 6 a.m.

So I tried something different. I told myself I would do exactly one push-up a day. One. That's it. Some days I did one push-up and went back to bed. Some days I did one and then thought, well, I'm already down here, and did five more. Some days I did twenty. But the rule was one. The rule was never more than one.

That was three years ago. I haven't missed a day since. Not because I'm disciplined — I'm not, I'm the guy with the cereal box — but because one push-up is so small that skipping it would feel more ridiculous than doing it. That's the whole trick. You make the habit so tiny that failure becomes harder than success.

This is the core idea of this entire book, so let me say it plainly: start with a habit so small you can't fail. Not small enough that you probably won't fail. Small enough that you literally cannot fail. One push-up. One page. One sentence in your journal. One glass of water.

You might be thinking, "That's too easy. What's the point?" And I get it. But here's what you're missing: the point isn't the push-up. The point is becoming the kind of person who doesn't skip. Every time you do your tiny habit, you cast a vote for your new identity. One push-up is a vote for "I'm someone who moves my body every day." One page is a vote for "I'm a reader." The votes add up. The push-ups add up too, by the way — I can do forty now, and I never once planned to get here.

There's a second reason this works, and it's sneakier. Big habits require motivation. Small habits require almost nothing. And motivation, if you haven't noticed, is a terrible employee. It shows up late, takes days off, and quits the moment things get hard. Tiny habits don't need motivation. They need a moment. You can do one push-up while the coffee brews. You can read one page while you're waiting for the microwave. You can write one sentence before you take your shoes off.

So here's your assignment. Pick one thing you want to do daily. Now shrink it until it feels almost embarrassing. Not "meditate for ten minutes" — "take three deep breaths." Not "run three miles" — "put on my running shoes." Not "write a novel" — "write one sentence." If you're not slightly embarrassed by how small it is, shrink it again.

You're not building the habit yet. You're building the habit of having the habit. The rest comes later. It always does.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
People ask about the routine like there’s a secret door. There isn’t. There’s a clock, a chair, and a willingness to be bored for three hours.

I’m up at six. Not because I’m virtuous—because at forty-eight my bladder doesn’t negotiate. Coffee first, the cheap dark roast, two cups, and I don’t check email until I’ve written something. That rule has saved more books than any outline I’ve ever made. You check email at six-fifteen and suddenly it’s nine and you’ve read three newsletters about productivity and written nothing but a passive-aggressive reply to your editor about the cover.

I write longhand for the first pass. Legal pads, the yellow ones, blue Bic pens—the cheap ones, ten for four bucks. People think that’s romantic. It’s not. It’s because the internet doesn’t live in a legal pad. I get about eight hundred words a day that way, sometimes twelve hundred if the scene’s already cooked in my head, sometimes two hundred if it isn’t and I sit there like a stump. Two hundred words is still a win. Zero is a loss, and I’ve had plenty of those. Anybody who tells you they’ve never had a zero day is selling something.

Around nine-thirty I type up what I wrote. That’s the part nobody talks about—the transcription. It’s tedious and it’s where half the real editing happens, because your hand is faster than your judgment and your judgment catches up when you’re typing. I cut maybe ten percent right there. Adverbs mostly. I hate adverbs the way some people hate geese. Fine, geese are okay. Adverbs, mostly not.

Lunch is a sandwich I make myself, and I eat it away from the desk. Standing up, usually, looking out the window at the neighbor’s dog, who is a menace and I love him. No working lunches. I did working lunches for a decade and all I got was heartburn and a reputation for being reachable.

Afternoon is for the business. Emails, contracts, the copyedit that’s due Friday, the blurb request from a writer I owe a favor to, the interview I agreed to in a weak moment. I cap it at two hours. Two hours, then I go for a walk. Three miles, same route, which sounds dull until you’ve had a plot problem unsnarl itself at the second milepost because you stopped staring at it. I’ve solved more third acts on that walk than at any desk. The trick is you can’t bring your phone. Bring your phone and you’re just a guy walking and scrolling like everybody else.

I’m back by four. I don’t write new words after four. I used to, in my twenties, and they were bad words—tired words, showing-off words. Now I might reread tomorrow’s scene, make a note or two. Then I’m done. Truly done. I cook dinner, I watch something stupid, I go to bed at ten like a farmer.

Five days a week. Saturdays I answer fan mail, because I still read it and I still answer it, and Sundays I don’t touch the book at all. Not a sentence. That day off isn’t a luxury, it’s maintenance—skip it and by Wednesday the sentences start to smell like a closed room.

The dirty secret is that it’s not inspiration, it’s attendance. You show up, you put in the hours, and roughly one day in five the work actually sings. The other four you’re laying pipe. But you can’t lay pipe on a schedule you keep abandoning, and the singing days don’t come to people who aren’t there when they arrive.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
Chapter 3: The Two-Minute Rule

The dumbbell weighed fifteen pounds. It might as well have been a boulder.

I remember standing in my garage on a gray January morning, staring at it like it owed me money. I'd just finished reading yet another book about transformation—the kind with bold promises on the cover—and I had decided, with the fervor of a man who has bought new workout clothes, that I was going to get strong. Not eventually. Now. Starting with a serious routine: forty-five minutes a day, six days a week.

Day one went fine. Day two went fine. On day three, my alarm went off at 5:30 a.m., and my body produced a single, clear thought: *No.*

I bargained. I'd work out after work. After work came, and I was tired. I'd work out tomorrow. Tomorrow came, and the dumbbell was still there, heavier now with the weight of my guilt. Two weeks later, I admitted the truth I've since seen in hundreds of people I've coached: I hadn't failed because I was lazy. I had failed because I'd designed a habit that required a hero, and most days I'm just a guy.

So I tried something almost embarrassingly small. The next morning, I walked to the garage, picked up the dumbbell once, and put it down. That was it. One rep. Thirty seconds, maybe. I felt ridiculous. But I also felt something else—I had done it. Nothing in me could say *I didn't.*

The next day, one rep again. And the next. By the second week, one rep felt like a joke, so I did three. Then five. A month in, I was doing a full set. Not because discipline had descended upon me like a dove, but because a tiny habit had quietly grown into a bigger one while I wasn't looking.

This is the heart of what I call the Two-Minute Rule: when you start a new habit, it should take less than two minutes to do. Read one page. Put on your running shoes. Write one sentence. Stretch your arms overhead. The habit must be so small that it feels almost pointless—and that's precisely the point.

Why does this work? Three reasons.

First, it removes the negotiation. Most failed habits don't die on the battlefield; they die in the argument we have with ourselves before we begin. When a habit is tiny, there's nothing to argue about. Two minutes requires no motivation, and motivation is a terrible employee—brilliant on the first day, gone without notice by the third.

Second, it makes identity the target, not the outcome. One page isn't going to finish a book, but it votes for the kind of person who reads. That vote—cast daily—is what changes you. As I tell the people I coach: every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become. Tiny habits are cheap, frequent votes.

Third, it's a doorway, not a destination. The two-minute version is the ritual of showing up. Once you're through the door—garage open, toes on the mat, page in front of you—continuing is easy. Starting is the hard part, and you've made starting nearly impossible to fail at.

So here's the practice for this week: take the habit you're trying to build and shrink it by 90 percent. Want to journal? Write one sentence. Want to meditate? Take one conscious breath sitting in your chair. Want to run? Lace up and step outside—you can come right back in. If it feels too easy, you've done it right. The goal is not the rep. The goal is the person who shows up, day after day, until showing up is simply who you are.

My dumbbell still sits in that garage. These days I lift far more than fifteen pounds. But I've never forgotten the morning I lifted it just once—because that was the morning the habit began. Not with a grand plan. With a rep so small I couldn't fail.

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
Start with your desk. It is the first place where clutter accumulates, and the first place where you can win. Look at what is in front of you right now. Every object on that surface is asking for a small piece of your attention, whether you realize it or not. A stack of papers you have not touched in weeks. Three pens, though you only ever use one. A mug, a cable, a receipt, a book you meant to read. None of these things are neutral. Each one is a tiny unfinished decision, and your mind keeps a running tally of them whether you like it or not.

So clear it. Not organize it, not buy a nicer tray for it, clear it. Take everything off the surface and put it somewhere else. Then put back only what you actually use every day. The computer, the lamp, the one pen, the notebook. Everything else has to earn its place or leave. If you are unsure about an item, put it in a box and date the box. If you have not opened it in a month, you will not miss what is inside. A clear desk is not about tidiness for its own sake. It is about giving your mind one less thing to track. When you sit down, there should be nothing between you and the work except the work itself.

Now open your inbox. You probably feel a small dread just reading that word. That dread is the honest signal of how much unresolved input you are carrying. Your inbox is not a to-do list, and it is not a storage unit. It is a doorway. Things should pass through it, not live in it. Start by admitting how much of it you will never read. Search for anything older than a few months and archive all of it without opening a single message. You will not regret this. Nobody's emergency from last year is still an emergency now.

Then deal with what remains using a simple rule: for each message, do one of four things. Reply if it takes two minutes or less. Delete it if it needs nothing from you. Send it to a task list if it needs real work. Archive it if it is reference material you might need later. What you must not do is leave it sitting there while you decide. Every message you leave in the inbox is a decision you have postponed, and postponed decisions pile up like snow. Aim for an empty inbox at the end of each day, not because emptiness is sacred, but because a full inbox is a full mind.

Finally, your calendar. This is where the real work begins, because your calendar is your life in disguise. Open it and look honestly. How many of these commitments would you make again today, knowing what you know now? Meetings that exist because they have always existed. Calls that could be an email. Standing appointments nobody remembers the reason for. Each one of these is a block of time you will never get back, and time is the only thing you are actually spending.

Go through the next two weeks and cancel or decline one thing for every three you keep. Protect at least one block of uninterrupted time each day, and defend it like an appointment with someone important, because it is. When someone asks for your time, do not say yes to be polite. Say you will check and get back to them, then check whether it truly matters. Your calendar should reflect your priorities, not your anxieties. An empty hour is not wasted time. It is room to think, and thinking is the work that everything else depends on.

Clear the desk, clear the inbox, clear the calendar. Not once, but as a practice. Clutter does not stay gone on its own. It creeps back the moment you stop paying attention. So build the habit of returning to empty, and notice how much lighter your attention feels when there is less of it holding you down.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
Chapter 7: Automating Your Savings So You Never Have to Think About It

Let me tell you about my friend Danny. Danny is one of the smartest people I know. He reads financial books. He listens to money podcasts. He can explain index funds to you at a barbecue. And for about three years, Danny saved almost nothing. Not because he didn't want to. He genuinely did. But every month, the same thing happened: money came in, life happened, money went out, and by the time Danny remembered he was supposed to transfer some to savings, there was nothing left to transfer. He was trying to save with willpower, and willpower is a terrible savings account.

Then Danny did one thing. He logged into his bank, set up an automatic transfer of $150 from checking to savings every payday, and then he closed his laptop and forgot about it. A year later he had $1,800 sitting there that he never once missed. He didn't feel disciplined. He didn't feel like he'd made sacrifices. He just felt like a guy with more money than before. That's the whole trick, and I want to be really clear about it: automation beats motivation every single time.

Here's why this works so well. When you save manually, you're making a decision every month, and every decision is a chance to talk yourself out of it. "This month is tight." "I'll start next month." "I deserve a little treat." Your brain is excellent at rationalizing, and it will use that talent against your savings account. But when the transfer happens automatically on payday, there's no decision to make. The money moves before you ever see it in your checking account, which means you can't spend what you don't notice. It's the financial equivalent of hiding cookies from yourself. If they're not on the counter, you don't eat them.

So how do you actually set this up? Start with the account. Keep your savings at a different bank than your checking, if you can. I'm serious. If your savings is one tap away in the same app, you'll tap it. A little friction is your friend. Many online banks also pay better interest, which is a nice bonus.

Next, pick your number. Don't overthink it. A common starting point is 10 to 20 percent of each paycheck, but if that feels impossible, start with $25 a week. The amount matters way less than the habit. You can always increase it later, and you should, every time you get a raise. When your income goes up, bump the automatic transfer before your lifestyle does. That way your savings grows and your spending stays put.

Then pick your timing. The best day to automate is payday, because the money is there before you've had a chance to spend it. Set the transfer for the same day your paycheck lands, or the day after. And here's a pro move: set up a second automatic transfer to a separate account for things like travel, gifts, or car repairs. These are the expenses that usually wreck a budget, and automating for them means they stop being emergencies.

One last thing. Check in once a quarter. Not once a week, not every day. Just peek at your accounts four times a year to make sure everything's running and to nudge your numbers up if you can. That's it. Ten minutes, four times a year.

The beautiful thing about automated savings is that it turns a behavior you have to remember into a system that runs without you. You don't need to be the most disciplined person in the room. You just need to set it up once and let it work. Danny isn't a savings superhero. He's just a guy who stopped relying on willpower and let the bank do the remembering. You can be that guy too.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
Let’s kill the sacred cow right now: time management is a lie you’ve been sold by people who want to sell you planners.

You can’t manage time. Time is the one thing that doesn’t give a damn about your color-coded calendar. It ticks at the same rate whether you’re crushing it or staring at a screen wondering why your brain feels like wet cardboard. Everyone gets 1,440 minutes a day. Warren Buffett. The guy sleeping under the overpass. You. The minutes are identical. The *output* is not. And the difference isn’t discipline. It’s juice.

I used to be a time-management junkie. Woke up at 5 a.m. Cold plunge. Three-page to-do list before sunrise. I scheduled my life in 15-minute blocks and felt like a Navy SEAL. You know what happened? By 2 p.m. I was a zombie with a great calendar. I’d “work” for six more hours and produce garbage. I was logging hours like a lawyer and outputting like an intern.

Here’s the number that changed my life: your brain gets roughly four to five hours of genuine high-octane focus per day. That’s it. Not eight. Not ten. Four or five, and that’s if you’re lucky and you slept well and nobody’s texting you about a “quick sync.” The rest of the day? You’re running on fumes and pretending. Everyone is. The open-plan office is a museum of people faking productivity on fumes.

So stop asking “How do I fit more into my day?” Start asking “When am I actually dangerous?” For me it’s 9 to 11:30 in the morning. That’s my prime window. Two and a half hours where I can write, think, build—do the work that actually moves the needle. I guard those hours like a junkyard dog. No meetings. No email. No “just a quick question.” You want my 9 a.m.? You can have my 3 p.m., when I’m useless anyway and mostly just nodding at you.

Notice what I did there? I didn’t manage time. I managed energy. I matched the hardest work to the hours when my tank is full, and I shoved the administrative sludge into the hours when I’m running on half a battery. The total hours didn’t change. The results did.

And for the love of everything, stop treating sleep like a weakness. You need seven to eight hours. Not six. Not “I’ll catch up on the weekend.” You won’t. Sleep debt compounds like credit card interest, and you’re paying it with your judgment, your patience, and your waistline. Every hour of sleep you steal to “get ahead” is an hour you’ll pay back at triple the rate the next day in fog and bad decisions.

Here’s your homework, and it’s embarrassingly simple. For one week, rate your energy at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 4 p.m. Just a number, one to ten. After seven days you’ll see a pattern so obvious it’ll annoy you. Then—and this is the part people hate—move your single most important task into your highest-energy window and defend it like your career depends on it. Because it does.

You don’t need more hours. You’ve got plenty of those. You need to stop spending your best ones on garbage.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Chapter 3: The Sushi Incident

The first thing you need to know about our office was that it had been a mattress store. The second thing was that we never got the smell out.

We told ourselves it was character. We told investors it was "scrappy." We told the fire marshal it was probably just the carpet. But everyone who walked through our door that first year—engineers, candidates, the occasional bewildered UPS driver—was hit with the same faint ghost of foam rubber and 1990s retail despair. We hung air fresheners like talismans. We bought plants that died within weeks, as if the building itself rejected anything that hadn't once been sold at a discount.

I thought about that smell the night of the sushi incident, because it's the same lesson, really: you can't cover up the truth of a place. You can only decide what to do with it.

Here's what happened. We had just closed our seed round—$1.2 million, which felt like a billion and also like nothing, because our burn rate suggested we had roughly fourteen months to become a real company or die. Our lead investor, a man named Hal who wore fleece vests to board meetings and had made his money in industrial fasteners, sent over a congratulatory gift: a sushi platter for the whole team. Forty-eight pieces. Enough for twelve people who had been eating instant ramen for six months.

The problem was that our head of engineering, Priya, had called a mandatory all-hands at 6 p.m. sharp. The problem was also that the sushi arrived at 5:55. And the third problem—the real one—was that our office had exactly one table, and it was covered in the guts of a decommissioned server that Priya had been "harvesting for parts" for three weeks.

So when Priya walked out to give her all-hands, she found eleven engineers standing in a loose semicircle around a sushi platter balanced on a filing cabinet, eating with their hands, in near-total silence, because we had no plates and no chopsticks and no one had thought to ask.

She looked at us for a long moment. Then she said, "This is the most pathetic thing I've ever seen. And I once worked at a company that went through a layoff *during* a holiday party."

Everyone laughed. Relief. But then she did something I'll never forget: she pulled up a chair, sat down in front of the filing cabinet, and started eating salmon nigiri with her fingers like the rest of us. And while we ate, she ran the all-hands. Roadmap. Metrics. The search indexing bottleneck that was going to kill us if we didn't fix it by Q3. All of it delivered between bites, with soy sauce on her thumb.

Here's the practical part, the part I wish someone had told me.

First: the ritual matters more than the food. That platter was a gift, and gifts are culture. If your team receives a gift—a bonus, a launch, a win—and treats it as an inconvenience to be processed, you've taught them that good things are just more work. Priya could have postponed the all-hands by twenty minutes. She chose instead to fold the gift into the ritual, and in doing so she told everyone: *we celebrate, and we work, and we do both together.*

Second: constraints reveal values. We had no plates. We had no table. We had one filing cabinet and a smell we couldn't fix. The team didn't complain—they improvised. That improvisation only happens if leadership improvises first. If Priya had stood there and said "who was supposed to order plates," the room would have learned that mistakes are punished. Instead she sat down on the floor, and the room learned that the work is the point.

Third, and this is the one I still think about: the sushi was raw fish on a filing cabinet in a former mattress store, and it was the best meal I had that year. Not because of the fish. Because of what it proved. We were a company of twelve people who could not afford plates, and we were going to out-build companies that had cafeterias.

Hal, our investor, called the next week to ask how the team liked the gift. I told him the truth: we ate it off a filing cabinet with our hands.

There was a pause. Then he said, "Good. That means you're spending my money on the right things."

He was right. We were. And the smell never did go away—but eventually, we stopped noticing it, which is a different thing entirely.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
You want to stay faithful. That's the first thing to understand about yourself — the fact that you're reading this means you've already made a choice, and that choice matters more than any single moment of temptation ever will. Faithfulness isn't a switch you flip once at the altar; it's a practice, like brushing your teeth or showing up to work. You do it daily, mostly in small ways, and the small ways are what keep the big things intact.

Start by being honest about what temptation actually is. It rarely arrives as a dramatic seduction. It shows up as a coworker who laughs at your jokes, a text conversation that gets a little too easy, a fantasy you replay on your commute. None of these make you a bad person. But you have to name them to yourself before they name you. The moment you start telling yourself "it's harmless," pay attention. Harmless is the word people use right before they do something that isn't.

Draw your lines early and draw them wide. Don't wait until you're standing at the edge to decide where the edge is. Decide now: what you don't talk about with other people, what you don't do alone with someone of the opposite sex late at night, what you don't keep secret from your spouse. Secrets are the currency of betrayal. If you find yourself keeping something from your partner because telling them would upset them, that's not protection — that's the beginning of a wall. Tear it down while it's still small.

But here's the truth nobody puts on the wedding card: staying faithful is only half the job. The other half is making your marriage worth being faithful to. A marriage that runs on duty alone will eventually starve. You have to feed it.

Feed it with attention. Not the distracted kind where you're nodding while scrolling your phone, but the kind where you look at your partner and actually see them. Ask questions you don't already know the answers to. What are they worried about this week? What made them laugh today? What do they wish you knew? You'd be astonished how many long marriages die not from betrayal but from two people who stopped being curious about each other.

Feed it with play. Remember what you did when you were first together — the stupid jokes, the long drives with no destination, the way you'd stay up talking until two in the morning. You don't have to recreate that exactly, but you do have to protect some version of it. Schedule it if you have to. A marriage with no play in it becomes a business partnership with shared laundry.

Feed it with repair. You will fight. You will disappoint each other. The couples who last aren't the ones who never hurt each other; they're the ones who get good at coming back. Say sorry without a but. Listen without planning your defense. And when you've been wronged, forgive on purpose, not because the feeling arrived on its own, but because you decided the relationship was worth more than the grudge.

Finally, guard your heart's loyalty in the ordinary hours. Faithfulness is built on Tuesday afternoons, not just Saturday nights. It's built in how you speak about your spouse when they're not in the room, in the gratitude you actually voice, in the small daily choice to be on their team. Do that, and the big choices take care of themselves.

You can do this. Not perfectly. But faithfully. And faithfully is enough.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
People ask me all the time how my husband and I have made it work for eighteen years, and I always want to say "pure spite and a shared Netflix password," but that's not quite true. The real answer is less sexy and more useful: we decided, early on, that faithfulness wasn't a finish line we crossed at the wedding. It's a daily practice. Like flossing. Except occasionally more fun.

Here's the thing nobody tells you. Staying faithful isn't mostly about resisting some dramatic temptation in a hotel bar. It's about the small stuff — the coworker who gets your jokes, the ex who likes your Instagram posts at 11 p.m., the fantasy you keep feeding because reality feels a little stale that week. I learned this the hard way. Years ago I had a work friend who made me feel witty and interesting in a way I hadn't felt at home in months. Nothing happened. But I noticed I was saving up my best stories for him, and that scared me more than any kiss would have. So I told my husband. It was awkward. He was hurt. But we talked, and we fixed the thing that was actually broken, which was us.

So here's my unscientific, deeply personal list.

1. Tell on yourself. The moment you notice you're hiding something — a text, a lunch, a feeling — say it out loud. Secrets grow in the dark. Drag them into the kitchen light and they shrink to normal size. My husband and I have a rule: no "little" secrets. It's saved us more times than I can count.

2. Feed your marriage before you're starving. Nobody strays from a full plate. I'm not talking about grand gestures. I'm talking about Tuesday. Did you ask about their day and actually listen? Did you laugh at their dumb joke? Did you touch their arm in the kitchen for no reason? That's the food. Keep serving it.

3. Flirt with your own spouse. This sounds obvious and it is not. Somewhere around year ten we became roommates who split the mortgage. So we started leaving notes. Stupid ones. I once put a Post-it on the coffee maker that said "you look hot in sweatpants." He kept it in his wallet for a year. Be ridiculous. Ridiculous is romantic.

4. Have the boring fight. The affair usually isn't about sex. It's about escape from the unspoken thing. The resentment you've been marinating for six years. Say the thing. It'll be a bad Tuesday night. You'll survive it. I promise the fight is cheaper than the silence.

5. Protect the friendship. Here's my hot take: your spouse should be your favorite person to talk to, not just the person you split chores with. If you'd rather text literally anyone else about your day, that's a five-alarm fire. Put down the phone. Look at them. Ask a weird question. "If you could only eat one food forever, what is it?" It's dumb. It works.

Look, I'm not a therapist. I'm a woman who once cried in a Trader Joe's parking lot because my husband loaded the dishwasher wrong. Marriage is long. It's a thousand small choices, and most of them are boring. But the boring ones are the faithful ones. Choose each other on the regular days. The rest takes care of itself.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Ten minutes. That’s it. Not twenty, not an hour, not some sunrise-and-incense routine you saw on a yoga influencer’s feed. Ten minutes, same time every day, and I’ll tell you right now—most of you won’t do it. You’ll do it for four days, feel a little calmer, get bored, and quit. That’s the honest truth about these things. The people who stick with it aren’t more disciplined than you. They’re just more fed up.

Here’s the whole practice. Sit down. Anywhere’s fine—a chair, the edge of your bed, the floor with a cushion under your butt. Keep your back straight-ish. Don’t make it a posture contest. Close your eyes or don’t. Set a timer for ten minutes so you’re not checking the clock like a nervous interviewee. Then breathe in through your nose and out through your nose. That’s it. Your breath doesn’t need to be deep or special. Don’t chase some mystical rhythm. Just breathe like a normal human and pay attention to the air going in and out.

Your mind will wander. It will wander constantly. You’ll be three breaths in and suddenly you’re replaying a conversation from Tuesday or making a grocery list or worrying about money. This is not failure. This is the practice. The moment you notice you’re gone—that noticing is the rep. You just did a bicep curl for your brain. So you come back to the breath. No commentary, no self-flagellation. Just come back. You might do this forty times in ten minutes. Great. That’s forty reps.

Now the blunt part. If you skip a day, you’re not "starting over." That’s nonsense language from app notifications. You just missed a day. Do it the next day. If you miss a week, same thing. The habit doesn’t shatter—you just stopped doing it for a while and can start again. And for the love of everything, don’t download a meditation app that wants $14.99 a month and plays you whale sounds. You don’t need it. You need a chair and ten minutes. This isn’t complicated. We just like to make it complicated because buying something feels easier than sitting still with our own thoughts.

What actually happens if you do this for, say, six weeks? You start noticing things. You catch yourself mid-spiral before you’re fully in it. You notice tension in your shoulders and drop them. You get a half-second of space between something annoying happening and your reaction to it. That half-second is worth more than most people admit. It won’t make you blissful. Some days you’ll sit down and be miserable for ten minutes straight. Those days still count. Especially those days.

One more thing. Do it in the morning if you can, before the day gets its hooks in you. Not because mornings are sacred—because if you wait until evening, you’ll be tired and you’ll blow it off. Pick a time, plant your butt, and breathe. Ten minutes. No candles required. No app. No special pants. Just you and the air that’s been there the whole time.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Chapter 7: Beyond the Position

 The Man Who Didn't Want a Discount

In my second year of consulting, I nearly lost a client because I was too good at my job.

The client was a mid-sized manufacturer negotiating a five-year supply contract with a parts vendor. The vendor's opening price was 18% above what my client wanted to pay. I did what any confident young negotiator would do: I built a meticulous cost model, benchmarked the vendor against three competitors, and walked into the meeting armed with a target of 12% below their opening number.

The vendor's lead negotiator, a soft-spoken man named Harold, barely glanced at my spreadsheet. He conceded a few points on payment terms, held firm on price, and the meeting ended in a polite stalemate. Over the next two weeks, we went back and forth. Harold gave ground in frustratingly small increments—never enough to close the gap. I couldn't understand it. My numbers were airtight. The competitor quotes were real. By any rational measure, Harold's price was too high.

Frustrated, I suggested we escalate. My client's VP of operations agreed to join the next session. And that's when everything changed. Within ten minutes, the VP asked Harold a question I hadn't thought to ask: "What's keeping you up at night on this account?"

Harold paused. Then he told us. His company had been burned two years earlier by a customer who signed a three-year deal, then cut volume by 60% in year two, leaving Harold's plant with idle capacity and a painful write-down. His board had since imposed an unwritten rule: never again commit capacity to a customer without guarantees. The price wasn't the issue. Harold was padding the deal to protect himself against volume risk—and what he actually wanted, more than a higher price, was a commitment he could take to his board.

We restructured the contract in an afternoon: a modest price increase in exchange for a volume floor with pre-agreed penalties for shortfalls. Harold got his guarantee. My client got a price 9% below where we'd started—better than anything my spreadsheet had produced. The deal closed the following week.

I learned more from that failure than from any success since: the number on the table is almost never the thing being negotiated. Harold wasn't fighting over price. He was fighting over risk, security, and his own credibility with his board. I had spent two weeks negotiating against a position when I should have been negotiating against an interest.

 The Iceberg Beneath the Position

Every demand you hear in a negotiation is a position—a surface answer to a question the other side hasn't fully articulated, sometimes even to themselves. Beneath it sits a structure of interests: security, autonomy, reputation, speed, fairness, relationships, avoiding loss. Positions are what people say they want. Interests are why they want it.

The practical consequence is stark: two negotiators can argue positions for hours and find no zone of agreement, while the same two people, once interests are on the table, can often invent options neither had considered. Harold and I were stuck because I was solving for the wrong variable.

So how do you get beneath the surface? Three habits matter more than any script.

First, ask questions that invite stories, not numbers. "What's keeping you up at night?" worked on Harold because it asked for a narrative, not a concession. Other versions: "How did this deal get structured the way it is?" "What would a great outcome look like for you six months from now?" "What happened the last time you were in a situation like this?" People reveal interests when they tell stories, and stories are where the real constraints live.

Second, listen for what I call the "load-bearing worry." In almost every negotiation, one concern carries disproportionate weight—the thing that, if unaddressed, makes every other term feel unsafe. Harold's volume risk was load-bearing; no price concession could have compensated for it. When you hear a concern repeated, hedged, or circled back to, treat it as structural. Ask directly: "If we solved that, would the rest of this get easier?"

Third, test your read before you build. Before designing a solution, summarize what you think the other side needs and ask them to correct you: "It sounds like certainty of volume matters more to you than the last few points of price—am I reading that right?" This costs nothing and prevents the expensive error I made: building an elaborate solution to a problem my counterpart didn't have.

The discipline is simple to state and hard to practice: before you negotiate the number, negotiate your understanding of the person across the table. Harold taught me that the cheapest concession in any deal is the one that solves a problem you took the time to discover.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
Getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth is less about luck and more about engineering the conditions for it. You don't need a big ad budget or a viral moment. You need a handful of people who trust you enough to tell someone else.

Start by defining exactly who your first customer is. Not a vague demographic, but a specific person with a specific problem. When you can describe your ideal customer in one sentence, you'll recognize them when they walk in, and more importantly, they'll recognize themselves in how you talk about your business. Word of mouth spreads fastest when the message is simple enough for a customer to repeat at a dinner party without getting confused.

Next, make your first ten customers ridiculously happy. Not satisfied, not pleased, but genuinely delighted. Overdeliver on something small and unexpected. Handwrite a thank-you note. Follow up a week later to ask how things went. Remember a detail they mentioned and bring it up next time. These gestures cost almost nothing, but they create stories. And stories are the currency of word of mouth. People don't recommend a business because it was fine. They recommend it because they have a story to tell.

Then, ask. This is where most small businesses stumble. You assume happy customers will naturally tell others, so you never actually request it. Don't leave it to chance. After you've delivered a great experience, ask directly: "If you know anyone who could use this, I'd be grateful if you passed my name along." Make it easy for them. Give them something to share, whether it's a simple referral card, a link, or just a clear sentence they can repeat. The easier you make the ask, the more likely it happens.

Build referral into your rhythms. Offer a genuine incentive if it fits your business, but be careful. Discounts and rewards can work, yet they sometimes cheapen the recommendation. The strongest referrals come from customers who genuinely want to help you. A small thank-you for a referral, like a credit or a gift, works best when it feels like appreciation rather than a transaction.

Go where your customers already gather. Word of mouth doesn't only happen one-to-one. Join the local business association, show up at community events, sponsor the little league team, answer questions in the online groups your customers frequent. When you're visible in the places your customers trust, their recommendations carry more weight because they can point to you as a known quantity.

Keep the conversation going after the sale. Most word of mouth is lost in silence. Send a short email a month later, share a useful tip, or check in on how they're using what you sold them. Every touchpoint is a chance to stay top of mind, and people recommend businesses they remember.

Finally, track how new customers find you. Ask every single one. Write it down. When you know which referrals and which relationships actually produce customers, you can do more of what works. Your first hundred customers won't come from a single clever campaign. They'll come from a hundred small moments of trust, repeated and passed along. Build those moments deliberately, and the referrals will follow.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
The first time I had to tell someone their work wasn't good enough, I hid in the stairwell afterward. Not because I was afraid of them. Because I was afraid of me. Of what I'd become: a person who makes other people feel small in conference rooms.

I'd been a manager for exactly eleven days.

Here's what nobody tells you: the feedback itself is rarely the problem. The problem is everything we wrap around it. The apology sandwich. The three-minute preamble about how much we value you as a person. By the time we get to the actual point, everyone's confused, nobody's heard anything, and the person leaves wondering if they still have a job.

I learned this the hard way, so you get the shortcuts.

1. Say it in the first thirty seconds.

Your brain hears "we need to talk" and immediately starts writing its own horror movie. Every sentence before the real one is a jump scare. So skip the build-up. "I want to talk about the Henderson deck" beats "Hey, so, how are things going, all good? Great, great. So there's something I've been thinking about..." One of those is feedback. The other is an anxiety delivery system.

2. Be specific or be quiet.

"Your communication needs work" is not feedback. It's a horoscope. Tell me what happened, when, and what the impact was. "In Tuesday's client call, you cut off the account lead twice, and she went silent for the rest of the meeting" — that's something a person can actually do something with. Vague criticism just makes people defensive, because they're defending against a ghost.

3. Aim at the work, not the human.

There's a difference between "this report had errors on page three" and "you're sloppy." One is a problem to solve together. The other is a permanent verdict on their character. Guess which one people remember at 2 a.m.

4. Assume they want to be good at this.

This one changed everything for me. My team lead — we'll call her Dana — once told me, "People don't come to work hoping to disappoint you." And I thought, huh. Because I'd been managing like everyone was a suspect. When you start from "they probably want to do well and something's in the way," feedback stops being a verdict and becomes a conversation. "Help me understand what happened with the timeline" hits completely different than "you missed the deadline."

5. Shut up after you say it.

This is the hardest one. I once gave what I thought was crisp, clear feedback and then, because the silence was unbearable, kept talking for another four minutes — re-explaining, softening, contradicting myself. By the end, the poor guy thought I was complimenting him. Say the thing. Then ask a question. Then let them talk. Their response is the whole point.

And here's the thing I wish someone had told me in that stairwell: honest feedback, delivered with care, is one of the most respectful things you can do for another person. Pretending everything's fine when it isn't? That's the morale killer. People can feel the gap between what you say and what you mean, and it makes them crazy.

I still get a knot in my stomach before hard conversations. That's normal. Do it anyway, do it kindly, and do it fast. The stairwell's not that comfortable.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
The year after my divorce, I did something that made absolutely no sense on paper. I bought a one-way ticket to Lisbon with a backpack, a laptop, and a heart that felt like a cracked coffee mug — still holding liquid, but leaking. Everyone thought I'd lost my mind. My mother asked, gently, whether I'd considered therapy instead. I had. I was doing both. But there was something I needed to learn that no couch in the world could teach me: how to be alone without being lonely. So I went.

The first month was brutal. I remember sitting on a stone step in Alfama, watching two old men argue about soccer in a language I barely understood, and feeling this wave of panic — what have I done, I'm forty-three years old, I have no plan. But here's the thing about being lost in a foreign city: you can't afford to spiral. You have to find breakfast. You have to figure out which bus goes to the beach. Small problems crowd out the big ones, and that's a gift. I learned to let the small stuff save me.

By month three, in a hostel in Marrakech, I met a woman named Ruth who was seventy-one and traveling alone after her husband died. She told me over mint tea that grief is just love with nowhere to go, and that you have to give it somewhere to land. So I started writing postcards to my ex — not to send, just to write. Twenty or thirty of them, all over Morocco. It sounds dramatic, but it worked. The love needed a mailbox, even if it was a drawer in my suitcase.

The travel itself taught me things I didn't expect. In Vietnam, I got food poisoning so badly I couldn't leave my hotel room for two days, and a stranger — the woman who ran the guesthouse — brought me rice porridge and sat with me while I cried about something that had nothing to do with my stomach. That's when I understood that help arrives in forms you never booked. You just have to stay open to it.

And there was the night in Chiang Mai when I realized I hadn't thought about the divorce in three whole days. Not because I was healed, but because I was busy — busy living. That's the thing nobody tells you. Healing isn't a moment of clarity. It's a series of afternoons where you forget to be sad because you're too interested in what's in front of you.

By the end of the year, I came home with a tan, a terrible haircut, and about four sentences' worth of wisdom that I'll keep forever. One: loneliness is a signal, not a verdict. Two: you can't think your way out of grief; you have to walk it out, or bus it out, or fly it out. Three: the world is full of people who will be kind to you if you let them, and that's worth more than any plan.

I'm not going to pretend the trip fixed me. It didn't. But it gave me a story where before I only had a wound, and there's a difference between those two things. A wound is something that happened to you. A story is something you made. That year, I made one. And I'd do it again — maybe with a slightly better backpack and definitely with more Pepto-Bismol.

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Chapter 7: The Ask

 The Conversation I Almost Didn't Have

I was twenty-eight years old, three years into a job I loved, and underpaid by roughly fifteen thousand dollars. I knew this because a colleague—a friend, really—had left his offer letter on his desk one afternoon when I stopped by his office. We had the same title. He had two fewer years of experience. The number at the top of that page rearranged something in my chest.

For six weeks, I did nothing. I told myself the timing was wrong. The company was restructuring. My manager seemed stressed. I rehearsed conversations in the shower and then talked myself out of them by breakfast. What finally moved me wasn't courage—it was a mortgage pre-approval that came back smaller than I'd hoped. I needed a raise, and the only way to get one was to ask.

I scheduled thirty minutes with my manager and spent two weeks preparing: a list of what I'd shipped that year, two comparable salaries I'd learned through careful conversation, and a specific number. The meeting lasted twenty-two minutes. My manager looked at my list, was quiet for a moment, and said, "Honestly, I think you're right. Let me see what I can do." Ten days later I had a 12 percent increase and a new title. The conversation I'd dreaded for six weeks took less time than my commute.

Here's what undid me: the fear was almost entirely fictional. My manager wasn't annoyed. The company wasn't offended. Nobody laughed. The worst outcome I'd imagined—a flat no—was survivable, and I hadn't even gotten that.

 Why Most People Never Ask

I've since learned my six weeks of avoidance were utterly ordinary. Study after study finds that roughly half of workers—and the share is even higher among women and people of color—have never asked for a raise. The reasons cluster into a few familiar patterns.

The belief that good work speaks for itself. It doesn't. Your manager is juggling forty priorities and does not have a running tally of your contributions. Compensation decisions happen in calibration meetings where the loudest, best-documented cases win. If you're not in the room making your case, someone else's case is being made for them.

Fear of the relationship. People worry that asking will make them seem greedy, ungrateful, or difficult. In my experience the opposite is true: managers expect these conversations. A well-prepared ask signals that you take your career seriously.

Not knowing the number. It's hard to ask for something specific when you don't know what's reasonable. This is solvable. Talk to peers, check salary surveys for your role and region, and use sites like Glassdoor or Levels.fyi as starting points, not gospel.

Waiting for the perfect moment. There is no perfect moment. Budgets are always tight somewhere. The best time to ask is when you have evidence—a completed project, a strong review, a new responsibility—and the second-best time is now.

 The Framework That Works

When you do ask, structure matters. Here's the approach I've used and coached others through:

1. Schedule a dedicated conversation. Don't ambush your manager in the hallway. Ask for thirty minutes and say what it's about.
2. Lead with value, not need. "I want to talk about my compensation given what I've taken on this year" lands better than "I need more money."
3. Bring evidence. Three to five concrete accomplishments with outcomes—revenue, time saved, problems solved.
4. Name a specific number. Research-backed, slightly above your target. "I'm looking for X" is far more actionable than "I'd like a raise."
5. Practice the silence. After you state your number, stop talking. The urge to fill the pause is strong; resist it.
6. Ask about the path. If the answer is no, don't storm out. Ask: "What would need to be true in six months for this to be a yes?" Get it in writing.

The raise I almost didn't ask for changed my income, but the bigger shift was internal. I stopped treating my compensation as something that happened to me and started treating it as something I negotiated. That shift compounds—through promotions, job offers, and every conversation since. The ask is a skill, and like any skill, it improves with practice. The only version that never works is the one you don't make.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
You do not need to clear your mind. You do not need to stop your thoughts. You do not need to sit in a special posture or wait until you feel calm before you begin. The practice of mindful breathing is far simpler and far kinder than most people expect. All you need is ten minutes and the willingness to show up.

Find a place where you can sit comfortably. A chair is fine. The edge of your bed is fine. Sit in a way that lets your spine feel upright but not stiff, and let your hands rest wherever they are comfortable. You can close your eyes or soften your gaze toward the floor. There is no perfect position, only one that lets you relax a little.

Now bring your attention to your breath. Notice where you feel it most clearly. It might be the cool air at the tip of your nose, the rise and fall of your chest, or the gentle expansion of your belly. Choose one of these places and let your attention rest there, like a hand resting on a windowsill. You are not forcing the breath to be deeper or slower. You are simply noticing the breath that is already happening.

Your mind will wander. This is not a problem. This is the practice. When you notice that you have drifted into planning, remembering, or worrying, you have just done the most important thing: you have noticed. Without judging yourself, gently return to the breath. You might say silently, thinking, and then come back. You may need to do this dozens of times in ten minutes. Each return is a small act of kindness toward yourself, not a failure.

You will likely discover that your thoughts are busy. That is normal. The goal is not to silence them but to stop being pulled along by every one. Imagine sitting on the bank of a river, watching thoughts float past. You do not have to climb into every boat. You can let them go and return to the steady rhythm of your breathing.

As you settle in, you may notice a sense of space opening up. The breath becomes a quiet anchor, something steady you can return to when the mind gets loud. This is where happiness begins to grow, not because anything dramatic happens, but because you are learning to be present with yourself without running away. You are giving yourself ten minutes of not needing to fix anything, achieve anything, or be anyone other than who you are right now.

When your ten minutes are up, take a moment before you stand. Notice how you feel. You may feel calmer, or you may feel restless. Both are okay. The benefits of this practice are cumulative, not instant. What matters is that you return tomorrow, and the next day, even if only for a few minutes. Consistency is worth more than intensity.

If you miss a day, simply begin again. There is no streak to protect, no perfect practice to maintain. Each session is a fresh start. You are training your attention the way you might train a muscle, gently and repeatedly, with patience rather than force.

Happiness is not something you chase in this practice. It is something you uncover by making room for stillness. Ten minutes a day is enough. Sit down, follow your breath, and come back when you wander. That is the whole practice, and it is enough.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
People always ask me what my writing routine looks like, and I think they're hoping for something glamorous. A cabin in the woods. A fountain pen. Maybe a muse who shows up at nine sharp wearing a velvet cape. The truth is my routine is mostly about snacks and avoiding my phone, and I've made peace with that.

Here's the thing nobody tells you when you pivot from blogging to novels: the internet does not care that you're writing a book. Your readers still want the Tuesday post. Your inbox still fills up. And somewhere in there you're supposed to produce 80,000 words about people who don't exist. My first month as a "real novelist," I answered email until noon every day and then wondered why my word count was zero. It turns out the blog had trained me to be instantly responsive, which is a lovely quality in a blogger and a catastrophic one in a novelist.

So I built a routine out of pure spite and mild desperation. I get up at six, which sounds virtuous until you learn I go to bed at nine like a Victorian child. I make coffee. I do not check my phone. This is the hardest part of my entire day, and I have written three books, so let that sink in.

1. Write before you read anything with a comment section. My rule is no internet until I've hit 500 words. Some mornings that means I'm writing garbage at 6:15 with one eye open. Fine. Garbage can be fixed. A blank page cannot be edited, and neither can a morning you spent arguing with a stranger about semicolons.

2. Keep the same chair. I'm not superstitious, but I am lazy, and my desk chair has a groove shaped exactly like me. Novel-writing is a war of attrition against your own distractions, and familiarity is a weapon. Same chair, same mug, same playlist of instrumental music that I've heard so many times it's basically white noise with feelings.

3. Stop while you still know what happens next. Hemingway said this and I'm paraphrasing because I'm a blogger at heart, but it works. If I write to the end of a scene and I'm stuck, I stop mid-sentence. The next morning I sit down and I already have a thread to pull. It's the cheapest trick in the business and I use it every single day.

The funny part is that my routine looks nothing like my blogging days, when I'd write at midnight with a laptop on my knees and a cat asleep on the keyboard. Now I have "office hours."
