My husband knows not to knock unless there's a fire or a package. My neighbors probably think I'm a very boring person who sits in a window and types, which is accurate.

And here's the secret nobody puts on the book jacket: the routine isn't about inspiration. It's about showing up so often that inspiration gets embarrassed and finally shows up too. I don't wait for the muse. I put out a chair for her, and if she doesn't come, I write without her, and honestly, some of my best chapters happened on days she ghosted me.

So that's the glamorous truth. Coffee, chair, 500 words, no internet, stop early. Repeat until the book exists. The velvet cape is optional.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
The year after my divorce, I did something that made absolutely no sense on paper. I bought a one-way ticket to Lisbon with a backpack, a laptop, and a heart that felt like it had been run over by a truck. My friends thought I was having a breakdown. My mother thought I was having a breakdown. Honestly, I wasn't entirely sure they were wrong.

But here's the thing about rock bottom: you get really clear about what you don't want. And I didn't want to sit in my empty apartment in Chicago, staring at the ghost of a marriage that had quietly died long before the paperwork caught up. So I left.

The first month was terrible. I'm not going to romanticize it. I cried in a hostel bathroom in Lisbon because I couldn't figure out how to work the shower. I ate dinner alone at restaurants where the waiters looked at me with pity. I called my sister at 3 a.m. her time, sobbing about how I'd made a huge mistake and should come home. She listened, and then she said something I'll never forget: "You're not lost. You're just somewhere new."

That became my mantra.

Traveling alone after heartbreak is like learning to walk again. Everything is unfamiliar, and unfamiliarity is both terrifying and oddly liberating. In Barcelona, I got hopelessly lost on my first day and ended up in a tiny neighborhood bar where an old man taught me how to order vermouth properly. We couldn't speak each other's language, but we laughed for two hours. I realized I hadn't laughed like that in years. Not because my ex was a monster, but because I'd been so busy maintaining a marriage that wasn't working that I'd forgotten how to be a person.

By month three, I'd developed a rhythm. I'd wake up, find coffee, work from a co-working space or a café, and then spend the afternoon wandering. I learned that I love markets—not the touristy ones, but the real ones where locals buy their vegetables and argue about prices. I learned that I'm terrible at reading maps but excellent at finding my way home by instinct. I learned that loneliness and solitude are two very different things, and somewhere between Portugal and Italy, I crossed the border from one to the other.

There's a specific moment I keep coming back to. I was in a small town in Tuscany, sitting on a stone wall at sunset, eating a peach that was so ripe it dripped down my chin. And I thought: I'm okay. Not great, not healed, not "over it" in any tidy way. But okay. I was sitting on a wall in Italy, eating the best peach of my life, and I was okay. That was the first time since the divorce that I believed I might actually survive it.

The lessons didn't come as lightning bolts. They crept in. I learned that grief has no itinerary—I could be fine for two weeks and then fall apart in a supermarket because I saw a couple arguing over cereal. I learned that asking for help isn't weakness; it's just good logistics. I learned that I'm more resilient than I gave myself credit for, and also more fragile. Both things are true.

When I came home after a year, I wasn't a new person. I was the same person, which was the real revelation. I hadn't needed to become someone else. I'd needed to remember who I was before I got lost in trying to be someone's wife. The travel didn't fix me. It just gave me enough distance to see that I wasn't broken.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
Here’s the thing about the twenty-eight-dollar avocado toast and the five-dollar latte. It’s a distraction. It’s a story we tell ourselves because it’s easier to feel guilty about a small, tangible, delicious thing than it is to confront the big, boring, structural stuff that actually determines whether we retire or work until we’re seventy-five.

I’m not saying money is infinite. I’m saying you’re optimizing the wrong variable.

Let’s do the math. A daily five-dollar latte, five days a week, fifty weeks a year—that’s $1,250. Okay. Now let’s say you’re forty-two and you’ve got $60,000 sitting in a 401(k) that’s mostly in a target-date fund with a 0.7% expense ratio, and you’re paying a financial advisor 1% a year to “manage” it. On a $60,000 balance, that’s $1,020 a year in fees. And that number grows as the balance grows. By the time you’re sixty-five, assuming 7% gross returns, that 1.7% combined drag could cost you well over six figures. Six figures. You could buy a latte every single day for the rest of your life and still come out ahead.

That’s the point. The latte is noise. The fee is a leak. The leak is what sinks the boat.

Here’s another one. You’re renting a two-bedroom for $2,400 a month because you “can’t afford to buy.” Meanwhile, your friend bought a starter condo three years ago at 6.5% interest and refinanced last spring. Their mortgage is $1,900. They’re not smarter than you. They just made a big, scary, leveraged bet on an asset that historically appreciates, while you made a series of small, safe, comfortable decisions that feel responsible but compound in the wrong direction.

I’m not telling you to buy a house if you don’t want one. I’m telling you to stop pretending that skipping the latte is a strategy. It’s a coping mechanism.

The big wins are unsexy. They’re renegotiating your salary once a year instead of clipping coupons. They’re maxing out the 401(k) match—which is literally free money, a 50% or 100% instant return—before you worry about whether you “deserve” the oat milk. They’re driving the car you already own for two more years instead of upgrading because the new one has ventilated seats. They’re choosing a partner who shares your financial values, because divorce is the single most efficient wealth-destruction tool ever invented.

And yes, they’re boring. Nobody writes a viral TikTok about increasing their 401(k) contribution rate by 2% and never thinking about it again. But that 2%—on a $70,000 salary, that’s $1,400 a year, plus match, plus thirty years of compounding—is a house. A real one. Not a latte.

So here’s my blunt opinion: the latte guilt is a scam. It’s a way to feel like you’re doing something without doing the hard thing. The hard thing is looking at your big three—housing, transportation, and taxes—and asking if you’re getting fleeced. The hard thing is having the awkward conversation about fees. The hard thing is admitting that your “safe” cash pile earning 0.4% while inflation eats 3% is a slow bleed, not a strategy.

Buy the latte. Or don’t. I genuinely don’t care. But if you’re going to feel guilty about something, feel guilty about the $18,000 you’re leaving on the table over the next decade because you never bothered to check what your advisor is actually charging you. That’s the number that matters. That’s the one that buys the house.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
Here is a draft for a personal finance book for young adults.

Let’s be honest about something: you are busy. Between work, school, trying to maintain a social life, and just surviving as a young adult, the last thing you want to do is remember to log into a banking app every single week to move twenty dollars from checking to savings. It is tedious, it is boring, and frankly, it is easy to forget. That is exactly why relying on willpower and memory is a trap. If you want to build wealth, you need to stop thinking about saving money as a task you perform and start thinking of it as a system you set up once and then ignore.

This is where automation comes in. Automation is the difference between hoping you save and knowing you save. When you automate your savings, you remove the human element—the procrastination, the temptation to spend, and the simple error of forgetting. You essentially pay your savings account before you ever have a chance to spend that money on takeout or a new video game.

Here is how you make this happen. First, you need to open a high-yield savings account if you haven’t already. Keep this account separate from your checking account. You want it to be slightly inconvenient to access, so you aren’t tempted to dip into it for a Friday night out. Once that account is open, you are going to set up an automatic transfer. This is a feature offered by virtually every bank and credit union.

Decide on a frequency and an amount that feels sustainable. If you get paid bi-weekly, set the transfer for the day after you get paid. Start with an amount that feels so small it is almost laughable. If you think you can save fifty dollars a week, start with twenty. The goal here is consistency, not heroics. You can always increase the amount later, but you want to get into the habit of seeing that money leave your checking account without panicking.

The beauty of this system is that it happens in the background. You don’t have to make a decision. You don’t have to check your balance and do mental math. The bank does it for you. After a few months, you will look at your savings balance and feel a genuine sense of surprise. It is like finding money in a coat pocket, except this is money you intentionally put there.

You should also automate your retirement contributions if your employer offers a 401(k) or similar plan. This is the ultimate set-it-and-forget-it move. You tell your employer to take a percentage of your paycheck and put it into your retirement account before you ever see it. Because it comes out of your gross pay, you never miss it. You just adjust your lifestyle to the slightly smaller paycheck. This is the easiest way to build long-term wealth because it requires zero ongoing effort from you.

The key takeaway here is that you should not be the one responsible for moving money around. You are a person with a life, and you will forget. The bank is a machine, and it will not forget. Let the machine do the work. Set up your transfers today, set a calendar reminder to check your balances in three months, and then go live your life. Your future self will thank you for the money you didn’t even have to think about.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
We had a ping-pong table before we had a business model. That tells you most of what you need to know about the early days. I joined as employee number eleven, which meant I got a desk made of a door and the title "Growth," a word that at the time meant "send emails and hope."

The office was above a nail salon. Every afternoon the fumes drifted up through the vents and we'd all get a little lightheaded and pitch increasingly unhinged ideas. That's how we ended up with a search feature nobody asked for that let you search *only* for pages that hadn't changed since your last visit. We called it "What's New?" It was, in retrospect, terrible. Two people loved it. One of them was the CEO's mom.

Our founder believed in what he called "productive chaos." This meant there was no org chart, no meeting schedule, and one single whiteboard that anyone could erase. I once came in to find my entire roadmap wiped and replaced with a drawing of a horse. I never found out who did it. I never asked. That's the culture in a nutshell — you learned not to ask.

A few things I wish someone had told me.

1. Your job title is a rumor. I was "Growth" for eight months before I found out I'd been reassigned to "Search Quality" because the founder wrote it on a napkin. Nobody told me. I just noticed my emails stopped getting replies from the engineering team and started getting replies from a guy named Deepak who kept sending me spreadsheets of "bad queries." I learned to love those spreadsheets.

2. Rituals beat processes. Every Friday at 4pm we'd stop and demo whatever we'd built, even if it was broken, especially if it was broken. This was sacred. It was also the only time the whole company was in one room. Eighteen people, one door-desk, a lot of half-finished bagels. The demos were mostly bad. But they were *ours*.

3. Hire people who laugh at the same things. Sounds soft. It's not. When you're debugging a crawler at 2am and someone makes a joke about how the internet is just "a series of tubes," and everyone groans — that's the glue. We once spent twenty minutes naming a server "Gary." Gary crashed constantly. We still loved Gary.

The weirdest part was how fast it stopped being weird. Six months in, I stopped noticing the nail salon smell. A year in, I couldn't remember what a normal office felt like. I'd go to a friend's company and see their quiet rows of monitors and think, where's the horse drawing? Where's the guy who plays trumpet at his desk when a deploy succeeds? (He only did it twice. It was amazing both times.)

We didn't know we were building something that would eventually index a good chunk of the human internet. We were just trying to make the search box not return a recipe for lasagna when you typed "how to fix a bike." Some days we succeeded. Most days we ate bagels and argued about Gary.

The company got big. The ping-pong table got replaced by a "wellness room." I left eventually. But I still search the way I learned to search there — impatiently, expecting the answer to be one keystroke away, annoyed when it isn't. And I still think about that horse. Whoever drew it, I hope you're well. You had vision.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Here's a chapter written in the style of a bestselling leadership book author — conversational, personal, and practical.

---

Chapter 7: The Conversation You're Avoiding Is the One That Matters Most

Let me tell you about the worst feedback I ever gave. It wasn't cruel. It wasn't loud. In fact, it was so soft that the person on the receiving end didn't even know they'd been given feedback. I sat down with a junior designer named Marcus, smiled, and said something like, "Hey, this is really solid work — I just wonder if maybe there's a version where the layout breathes a little more?" He nodded, said thanks, and went back to his desk and changed nothing. Of course he didn't. I hadn't told him anything. I'd told him a feeling.

Three months later, Marcus was blindsided in a performance review. He genuinely believed he was doing great work, because every conversation we'd had was soft enough to be mistaken for encouragement. That's on me. I thought I was being kind. I was actually being cowardly, and my cowardice cost him months of growth.

Here's the truth nobody tells new managers: vague praise and vague criticism are the same thing. Both leave people confused. Both are a way of protecting yourself instead of serving the person in front of you.

So how do you give honest feedback without crushing someone's spirit? Let me give you the framework I wish someone had handed me.

First, separate the behavior from the identity. "You missed two deadlines this month" is a behavior. "You're unreliable" is an identity. The first gives someone something to work with. The second gives them something to defend against. When people feel their identity is under attack, their brain goes into threat mode and the learning centers shut down. Literally — this is neuroscience, not just vibes. So be surgical about the behavior and generous about the person.

Second, lead with your intent, out loud. Before you deliver the tough message, say why you're saying it. "I'm telling you this because I think you're capable of more, and I don't want you to be surprised by anything down the road." That one sentence changes the entire temperature of the room. It tells them you're on their side before you've even said the hard part.

Third, be specific and timely. Feedback delivered three weeks after the fact is a history lesson, not a coaching moment. And "be more proactive" means nothing. "In Tuesday's client call, you waited for me to answer three questions that were directed at you — next time, jump in, even if you're not 100 percent sure" — that means something. Vague feedback feels safer to give, but it's actually more brutal to receive, because there's no way to act on it.

Fourth — and this is the one that took me years — ask before you unload. "Can I give you some direct feedback on that meeting?" Ninety percent of the time, people say yes. And when they say yes, they've consented to hear it. You've turned a verdict into a conversation.

Finally, close the loop with belief. After the hard part, say what you see in them. Not as a consolation prize, but as the truth. "This is a fixable thing, and I'm telling you because I think you're going to be really good at this." People can handle almost any truth when they know you believe in them.

Look, new managers — the goal isn't to avoid discomfort. The goal is to be the person who tells people the truth early, kindly, and specifically, so they're never blindsided. The leaders who crushed my morale weren't the ones who were honest with me. They were the ones who weren't. Be honest. Be specific. Be on their side. That's the whole job.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Most people walk into a negotiation and start arguing about the number. Wrong move. The number is the last thing you should touch. The number is just the receipt for a bundle of wants underneath it, and until you know what's in that bundle, you're bidding blind.

Here's what I mean. A vendor quotes you $180,000 for a software rollout. You counter at $140,000. He comes back at $165,000. You settle at $158,000 and both of you walk away feeling vaguely robbed. Congratulations — you just spent three weeks haggling over the price of a thing neither of you actually understood.

Now flip it. Before you talk money, you ask one question: "Walk me through how you arrived at that figure." Not accusatory. Curious. And then you shut up. I mean it — count to ten in your head if you have to. Most negotiators fill silence because it makes them nervous. That silence is where the money is.

The vendor starts talking. Turns out $40,000 of that quote is a training package you don't need because your team already knows the platform. Another $15,000 is "implementation support" that's really just two guys on a phone for a month. But here's the thing — he's got a quarterly quota, and it's March 28th. That quota is a want he'll never put on a slide.

That's the whole game. People tell you what they want you to hear. Your job is to find the want they're trying to hide — from you, sometimes from themselves.

I learned this the hard way selling commercial real estate in my twenties. Had a landlord dead to rights on an empty building, six months of carrying costs bleeding him dry. I went in cocky, lowballed him, and he walked. Found out later he didn't care about the price at all — he needed the deal to close before year-end for tax reasons. I could've paid his full asking price in November and still won. Instead I lost the building to a guy who asked better questions than I did. Cost me about $60,000 in commission. Cheap tuition, in hindsight, but it stung.

So how do you actually do it? Three moves.

First, ask about priorities, not positions. "If you could wave a wand and fix one thing about this deal, what would it be?" Positions are "$165,000." Priorities are "I need this off my books by Q3." Big difference.

Second, listen for the words they repeat. People leak their real concerns through repetition. If he mentions "timeline" four times in a fifteen-minute call, price is probably flexible and schedule isn't. I've seen deals close at 20% over market because the buyer needed speed and the seller needed certainty, and neither one ever said so out loud until somebody asked.

Third — and this is the one nobody likes — go first on generosity. Offer something cheap to you and valuable to them before you ask for anything. A flexible payment schedule. A case study you'll let them publish. Public credit. It costs you almost nothing and it buys you information, because people relax when they feel heard, and relaxed people talk.

The amateurs think negotiation is a contest of wills. It's not. It's a contest of curiosity. The person asking the better questions wins, almost every time.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
Chapter 7: The Geometry of Grace

I spent the first decade of my adult life trying to build a life that looked impressive on paper. I had a five-year plan, a ten-year plan, and a color-coded spreadsheet to track my progress toward both. My faith was real, but it was also neatly compartmentalized—a Sunday affair that coexisted peacefully with my ambitions the rest of the week. I believed in serving others, in theory. I just assumed it was something I would get to *after* I had built a life worth sharing.

Then my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, had a stroke.

He was a widower in his late seventies, a retired machinist with a gruff exterior and a meticulously kept rose garden. We had exchanged perhaps a hundred words in the three years we’d lived next door to each other. When he came home from the hospital, his daughter—who lived six hours away—called me in a panic. Could I just check on him? Maybe bring in his mail?

I said yes because it felt like the Christian thing to do, but I confess my heart wasn’t in it. I was busy. I had deadlines. I had a life to build. The first few weeks, I treated the task like another item on my to-do list: *Drop off groceries. Pick up prescriptions. Get back to work.*

But something strange happened in the geometry of those small, inconvenient acts. I started staying a few minutes longer. Mr. Henderson, a man of few words, began to talk. He told me about the roses—how each one was a cutting from a bush his wife had planted forty years earlier. He told me about the war, about the factory, about the son he’d lost too young. I told him about my job, my stress, my carefully plotted future. He listened with a stillness that felt like a rebuke to my franticness.

One Tuesday, as I was leaving, he grasped my hand. His grip was still weak from the stroke. “You know,” he said, his voice a rasp, “I’ve been praying for years that God would send someone to just… be here. I didn’t think it would be the busy young man next door.”

I walked home and sat in my car in the driveway for a long time. I thought about my spreadsheet, my plans, my impressive-on-paper life. And I realized that in all my striving, I had been building a monument to myself. It was sturdy, yes. But it was empty. The only things that had felt truly real in months were the moments spent in that dim living room, listening to an old man talk about roses. I had set out to be the answer to someone’s prayer, and God had used it to answer mine.

This is the paradox Jesus spoke of: “Whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will find it” (Matthew 16:25). We think meaning is a destination we reach by accumulating achievements. But meaning is a byproduct of love. It is found in the losing—the losing of our time, our plans, our precious schedules—for the sake of another.

Here is the practical truth I learned from Mr. Henderson: Serving others is not a grand, sweeping gesture. It is a series of small, faithful obediences. You do not need to find a cause or a calling. You need only to look at the person God has placed directly in front of you.

Start with your own street. Your own office. Your own family. Ask God to show you one person—just one—who needs a small act of grace this week. Then do it. Bring the meal. Make the call. Sit and listen. And when your schedule screams at you to leave, stay five minutes longer.

The path to a meaningful life is not a ladder you climb. It is a circle you draw around someone else. In that circle, the frantic striving quiets, and you discover that you were never building a life at all. You were being invited into one.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
People ask me all the time how my husband and I have made it work for eighteen years, and I always want to say: mostly luck, plus the fact that neither of us has the energy to start over. But that's not a book, so let me try to be useful.

Here's the thing nobody tells you: marriage is not a romantic comedy. It's more like a group project that never ends, except your partner actually does the work and you can't just email the professor to switch teams. The vows are easy. The Tuesday nights are hard.

I remember early on, maybe year three, when we were in that phase where everything my husband did annoyed me, including breathing. I called my mom and said, "I think I married the wrong person." She laughed and said, "You did. So did I. Now go make dinner." Not exactly Chicken Soup for the Soul, but honestly? Best advice I ever got. The "wrong person" myth has ruined more marriages than infidelity ever has.

Which brings me to staying faithful, the part everyone whispers about. Here's my hot take: faithfulness isn't a feeling. It's a series of small, boring decisions you make before the feeling ever shows up. You don't wake up one day and decide to have an affair. You decide to text back. You decide to linger. You decide to tell a stranger something you haven't told your spouse. That's the door. The affair just walks through it.

So here are a few things that have actually worked for us.

1. Talk about the awkward stuff before it's a crisis. We have a rule: if you're tempted, you tell me. Not as a confession, as a heads-up. Like weather reporting. "Hey, it's flirty at the office today, expect some drizzle." Sounds insane. It works. Secrets grow in the dark. Drag them into the light and they shrivel.

2. Flirt with your own spouse. I know. Revolutionary. But somewhere around year ten, people stop flirting with each other and start flirting with the idea of a vacation from each other. Send the dumb text. Grab the butt in the kitchen. Be a little ridiculous. Ridiculous is the opposite of roommates.

3. Have a life that isn't just the marriage. The couples I see struggle the most are the ones who made each other their entire personality. That's too much weight for one person to carry. Go have friends. Have hobbies. Come home with something to say that isn't about the dishwasher.

4. Fight better. We used to fight to win. Now we fight to finish. There's a difference. Winning means someone sleeps on the couch and both of you lose. Also, and I cannot stress this enough, learn to say "I was a jerk" without the word "but" attached to it. The "but" ruins everything. "I was a jerk, but you—" no. Just be a jerk and own it.

5. Protect the ordinary. This is the unsexy one. Make the coffee. Fill the gas tank. Remember the thing they mentioned once in passing. Love lives in the boring details. Grand gestures are for anniversaries. Tuesday is for showing up.

Look, I'm not a therapist. I'm a woman who once cried in a Target parking lot because my husband bought the wrong kind of salsa, and I'm still married to him. That's my credential. The bar is lower than you think, and the work is smaller than you fear. Stay curious about each other. Keep the door closed. And for the love of everything, put your phone down at dinner.

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
The hiring mistake that nearly sank the company didn't announce itself as a mistake. It walked in wearing a beautiful suit, with a Harvard MBA and a track record that made my board drool. Let me call him David. Within six months, I knew I'd made the worst call of my career — and by then, he'd already hired three people just like him.

Here's the thing nobody tells you about being a CEO: by the time you're running the place, you've usually gotten pretty good at judging people. Or so you think. I'd built my first company from eight people in a garage to four hundred employees, and I prided myself on gut instinct. I could spot a phony in a fifteen-minute coffee. But David? David was my blind spot. He was brilliant, articulate, and — this is the part that hooked me — he agreed with me. On everything. In interviews, he finished my sentences. He told me exactly what I wanted to hear about scaling operations, about the European expansion, about the culture I was trying to protect. I walked out of that final interview thinking I'd found my co-pilot. What I'd actually found was a mirror.

The trouble started small. David reorganized his division without telling anyone outside it. Then he stopped coming to the Monday leadership meeting — sent a deputy instead, a guy who took notes and said nothing. When I finally cornered him, he smiled and said, "I'm protecting your time, Jack. You should be thinking about the next five years, not the next five weeks." It sounded generous. It was a coup in slow motion. By month eight, his division had its own all-hands, its own metrics, its own vocabulary. People started calling it "the silo," and they weren't joking.

Then the real damage hit. We lost our biggest enterprise client — a relationship I'd personally built over seven years — because David had promised them a custom integration our engineers couldn't deliver. He hadn't checked with engineering. He hadn't checked with me. He'd just wanted the win, and he'd wanted it to be his win. When I confronted him, he didn't apologize. He explained. He explained for forty minutes. And somewhere in that monologue, I realized I was listening to a man who genuinely believed the company existed to serve his résumé.

Firing him took three weeks and cost us two senior engineers who'd been loyal to him, plus a chunk of my own confidence I'm still not sure I've fully recovered. But the real cost was the lesson, and the lesson was this: I hadn't hired a bad person. I'd hired a person who was bad for us, and I'd done it because I confused chemistry with character. David and I had chemistry. What we didn't have was a single honest disagreement in six months of working together — and that, I now know, is not a sign of alignment. It's a warning siren.

So here's what I tell every CEO who asks me about hiring now, usually over a drink and usually after they've already made the mistake: stop hiring people who make you feel smart. Hire the ones who make you think. The best people I ever brought in argued with me in the interview. One of them — my eventual successor — told me my five-year plan was "optimistic to the point of fantasy." I hired her on the spot. She was right, by the way. She usually was.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
The First Hundred: Word of Mouth Isn’t a Strategy, It’s a Consequence

Let me save you twelve months and about forty thousand dollars: nobody talks about your business because you asked them to. They talk because something happened that they couldn’t not talk about.

I learned this the hard way with my second company. First company, I did everything the books say—referral cards, “tell a friend” discounts, a loyalty program with the graphic design budget of a small country. You know how many customers that got me in six months? Nine. And four of them were my cousins.

Second company, I stopped asking and started engineering. Hundred customers in ninety-one days, zero dollars on ads, and I’ll tell you exactly what we did.

First, we picked a number: 100. Not “grow the business.” A hundred paying customers, by name, on a list. Vague goals get vague effort. If you can’t count it, you’re not running a business, you’re journaling.

Then we got brutally honest about who talks. Not who buys—who *talks*. In every category there’s a small tribe of people who get asked for recommendations: the barber everyone trusts, the office manager who knows every caterer in town, the guy in the neighborhood Facebook group with 4,000 posts and zero chill. We listed forty of them by name. Forty. Took a weekend. Then we gave each one a reason to talk that wasn’t money.

Here’s where most small businesses screw up: they pay for referrals. Cash for a lead cheapens the relationship. Your customer isn’t a sales rep, and the second you treat them like one, the recommendation sounds like a pitch. What we did instead was make the *thing itself* remarkable. Our product had one feature nobody else had—one, not five—and it was the kind of feature you have to explain, which meant every customer who loved it had to tell someone else what it was. Confusion is a word-of-mouth engine. “Wait, it does what?” is the best marketing copy ever written, and it’s free.

We also asked at the right moment, not the wrong one. Not at checkout. Not in a follow-up email three days later with a smiley face. We asked at the moment of peak delight—right after the thing worked, when relief was still on their face. One sentence: “Who else do you know who’s dealing with this?” Not “please refer us.” Not “share the love.” A specific question about a specific problem. People answer specific questions. They ignore generic ones.

Numbers matter here, so here are mine. Out of 100 customers, 61 came from someone who was already a customer. Of those 61, 44 traced back to just eleven people. Eleven. Word of mouth isn’t a broad fog—it’s a handful of humans doing heavy lifting. Find your eleven. Feed them. Not with discounts. With early access, with insider info, with the thing they can brag about knowing first.

And for the love of everything, make it easy. If someone has to hunt for your name to text a friend, you’ve lost. We put our name on the product in a font you could read from across a room. Sounds stupid. It doubled our mentions.

One more thing, and this one stings: word of mouth amplifies whatever’s already there. If your service is mediocre, you’re just speeding up the bad news. The hundredth customer should get a better experience than the first, or you’re not building anything—you’re running a leaky bucket with a nicer label.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
The Latte Isn't the Problem

The first time I felt genuinely ashamed of a purchase, it cost me four dollars and fifty cents. I was twenty-six, working an entry-level marketing job, and I had just bought my usual Friday morning latte when a personal finance article landed in my feed. The headline informed me that my daily coffee habit would cost me over a million dollars by retirement, compounded at seven percent. I sat in my car doing the math three times, convinced I had ruined my life with foam.

Here's what that article never told me: I was also paying $340 a month for a car I barely drove, because I'd let a salesman talk me into the upgraded trim. I was paying $180 a month for a gym I'd visited four times since January. And I was paying an extra $95 a month in auto insurance because I'd never bothered to compare quotes. Nobody writes viral articles about those. They don't fit on a poster.

That year, I did what the guilt told me to do. I gave up the lattes. I bought a $12 drip coffee maker, drank bitter office coffee for eight months, and saved roughly $900. I felt virtuous. I felt miserable. And then in March, my car's transmission failed, and because I'd never built an emergency fund—because I'd been busy optimizing coffee instead of looking at the actual structure of my finances—I put the $2,400 repair on a credit card at 22 percent interest. The lattes didn't cause that. The absence of an emergency fund did, and no one was writing think pieces about that.

Here's the math that changed how I think about money. Give up a $4.50 latte every workday for a year and you save about $1,170. Genuinely meaningful—I'm not dismissing it. But renegotiating your car insurance, refinancing a student loan, or simply calling your internet provider to ask for the promotional rate can save $300 to $800 in a single afternoon. Maxing out an employer 401(k) match—free money you're literally leaving on the table—can be worth thousands annually. Moving $10,000 from a 0.01 percent savings account to a 4 percent high-yield account earns you $400 a year for perhaps twenty minutes of work. One decision, made once, outperforms a year of daily deprivation.

The latte myth persists because it's a story about individual virtue, and virtue stories are comforting. They suggest that financial health is a matter of character, of small daily discipline, of denying yourself small pleasures. That framing sells books and generates clicks, but it quietly lets the big stuff off the hook. It's much easier to feel guilty about a croissant than to confront the fact that you've never asked for a raise, that your investment fees are eating 1.5 percent annually, or that you're paying for three streaming services you forgot exist.

So here's what I want you to do this week. Pull up your last two bank statements and highlight every recurring charge over $50. Not the coffees—the subscriptions, the insurance premiums, the loan payments, the memberships. That's where your leverage lives. Then pick the single largest one and spend thirty minutes doing one of three things: cancel it, renegotiate it, or comparison-shop it. That's it. One thirty-minute session.

And then—this is the part I mean sincerely—buy the latte. Sit down with it. Enjoy it without a side of shame. Because the four dollars was never the problem, and treating it like the problem kept me from noticing the four hundred dollars hiding in plain sight every single month. Guilt is a terrible financial advisor. Attention is a much better one, and it costs nothing to give.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
You have been lied to about time. For years, the world has told you that the secret to achievement is a better calendar, a sharper to-do list, a more ruthless schedule. Wake up earlier. Work later. Optimize every minute. And yet, here you are, with a calendar full of commitments and a body full of exhaustion, wondering why the big goals still feel so far away.

Here is the truth that changes everything: you do not manage time. Time passes whether you manage it or not. What you actually manage, or fail to manage, is your energy. Two people can sit at the same desk for the same eight hours. One produces brilliant, focused work. The other stares at a screen, rereads the same paragraph five times, and ends the day with nothing to show but a headache. The difference is not time. It is energy.

Think about the last time you made real progress on something that mattered to you. Were you running on fumes, or were you fully alive, alert, and engaged? You already know the answer. Your best work never comes from your longest hours. It comes from your fullest ones.

So stop asking, How do I fit more into my day? Start asking, How do I bring more to my day?

This shift begins with a simple recognition: your energy is not infinite. It is a resource, and like any resource, it must be invested wisely. You have four accounts to draw from: your physical energy, your emotional energy, your mental energy, and your sense of purpose. Long-term goals are not built by draining one account to fuel another. They are built by keeping all four replenished and spending them deliberately.

Guard your body first. No goal survives a body that is starved of sleep, movement, and nourishment. You cannot think your way out of a physiological deficit. The walk you take, the water you drink, the sleep you protect, these are not indulgences. They are the foundation on which every ambitious thing you want to build rests.

Then protect your emotions. Resentment, worry, and self-criticism burn energy faster than any workout. Notice what drains you and have the courage to name it. Surround yourself with people who fill your tank rather than siphon it. The goal is not to feel good all the time. The goal is to stop leaking energy on things that do not matter.

Your mind needs rhythm, not just effort. Focus is a muscle, and it fatigues. Work in concentrated bursts, then truly rest. The most productive people you admire are not working every waking hour. They are working in alignment with their natural cycles, and they are ruthless about recovery.

Finally, connect your daily effort to something larger than the task itself. Purpose is the renewable fuel. When you know why a goal matters, you can endure far more than you thought possible.

Here is your new measure of a good day. Not, Did I check every box? But, Did I spend my energy on what matters most? Did I finish the day with something left to give to the people I love?

Your goals are not waiting for more hours. They are waiting for the fullest version of you. Protect your energy. Spend it with intention. And watch how far you go.

title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
Here's a chapter written in the voice of a bestselling productivity author:

Chapter 7: Single-Tasking in a World Built for Distraction

I want to tell you about the day I finally broke up with my own brain. It was a Tuesday. I was on a call, answering a Slack message, and half-watching a YouTube tutorial on how to dice an onion, all at the same time. And then my four-year-old walked in, tugged my sleeve, and asked me a question. I have absolutely no memory of what she said. None. I looked down at her little face, waiting for an answer, and I felt something cold in my chest. I had been "there" all morning. And I hadn't actually been there for a single second of it.

That's the dirty little secret of multitasking. It doesn't make you faster. It makes you absent.

Here's what's actually happening in your head when you try to do three things at once. Your brain isn't running three programs side by side like some kind of supercomputer. It's switching. Rapidly. Constantly. And every single switch costs you something. Researchers call it "attention residue" — a fancy term for the fact that when you jump from your email to that report, a chunk of your mind stays stuck on the email for a while. You're not fully in the report. You're half in the report and half still reading that subject line about the budget thing. So you do the report worse. And slower. And then you go back to email and do that worse too. It's like trying to have two conversations at once at a party. You don't get twice the conversation. You get two people who think you're rude.

I know what you're thinking. "But my job requires it." Look, I've been there. I once bragged about answering emails during conference talks. I thought I was being efficient. I was being an idiot with a laptop. Because here's the thing nobody tells you: the world isn't built for distraction by accident. It's built for distraction on purpose. Every app on your phone has a team of very smart people whose entire job is to get you to pick it up again. The notifications, the red badges, the little dopamine hit when someone likes your post — none of that is an accident. You are not weak for getting distracted. You are outnumbered.

So what do we do about it? We fight back with boring, unsexy, wildly effective single-tasking. And I mean single-tasking like your life depends on it.

Here's my rule, and it's embarrassingly simple: one thing at a time. Not two. One. When I'm writing, I'm writing. The email tab is closed. The phone is in another room — not face down on the desk, another room, because I know myself. When I'm in a meeting, I'm in the meeting. I take notes on paper because paper doesn't have a notification tray. When I'm with my daughter, I'm with my daughter. That's it. That's the whole trick.

Let me give you a concrete example, because I know "focus more" is useless advice. Last month I had a project I'd been avoiding for weeks — a big, ugly, important piece of work. I'd been "working on it" for days while also doing everything else, and it was going nowhere. So one morning I tried something radical. I put my phone in a drawer in another room. I closed every tab except the document. I set a timer for forty-five minutes. And I told myself: nothing else exists until this timer goes off. Forty-five minutes. That was it.

You know what happened? I got more done in those forty-five minutes than I had in the previous three days combined. Not because I'm special. Because I finally let my brain do one thing. It felt almost physically uncomfortable at first, like my hand kept twitching toward a phone that wasn't there. But by minute ten, something clicked. The work got easier. The words came faster. I was in it.

And that's the part nobody tells you about single-tasking. It's not just about getting more done. It's about getting to actually be there while you do it. When you single-task, you get your attention back. And your attention is the most valuable thing you own. You can't buy more of it. You can only stop giving it away for free.

So here's your homework. Pick one thing today — just one — and give it your full attention for twenty minutes. No phone. No tabs. No "just checking." Watch what happens. You might be shocked at how much you get done. You might be even more shocked at how good it feels to be fully awake in your own life again.

That's the whole game. One thing. Then the next. That's how you get it all done.

title: time-management book|saying no to good opportunities to protect great ones
text:
The 3% Rule

Here's what nobody tells you about good opportunities: they're the most expensive thing you'll ever own.

Not bad ones. Bad ones are easy. You can smell a bad opportunity from a mile away — the "exciting startup" that wants you for equity, the committee that needs "just a few hours a month." You say no to those without breaking a sweat.

It's the good ones that kill you. The podcast invite from someone you actually admire. The board seat at the nonprofit doing genuinely great work. The consulting gig that pays well and the client's not a jerk. These are the opportunities that make you feel like an idiot for hesitating. And that's exactly why they're dangerous.

I want you to do a brutal audit of last year. Pull up your calendar. Count the things you said yes to that were, on paper, good opportunities. I'll wait.

Now here's the number that should scare you: most of the people I've coached through this exercise find that 60 to 70 percent of their time went to opportunities they rated a 7 or an 8 out of 10. Not a 9. Not a 10. Sevens and eights. Solid. Respectable. Completely forgettable.

And here's the math that changed my life. If your calendar is 70 percent full of 7s and 8s, you have 30 percent left for the 10s. That's it. The great opportunities — the book you've been meaning to write, the product that could redefine your company, the actual deep work — are competing for scraps. You didn't say no to them. You just never had room.

The 10s don't announce themselves with fanfare. They look riskier. They pay less, at first. They don't come with a title or a nice LinkedIn post. They require you to bet on yourself in a way that a 7 never does. So when a 7 shows up with a deadline and a flattering email, it wins by default. Not because it's better. Because it's *scheduled*.

I have a rule now, and it's saved me more hours than any productivity app ever has: I don't say yes to anything that's an 8 or below, no matter how good it looks, until I've asked one question. *What 10 does this crowd out?* Not "is this worth my time" — that's the wrong question, and it's how you end up with a calendar full of worthwhile things that add up to a life you didn't choose. The question is what this displaces. If I can't name the 10, I don't take the 8.

Some of you are going to argue that this is arrogant. That you can't just turn down good things. Fine. But let me ask you something: when was the last time a 7 turned into a 10? Be honest. Most of them don't grow. They just take up space, and they're very polite about it.

Your yes is a finite resource. You get maybe four or five genuinely great opportunities a decade — the ones that actually change your trajectory. Five. Out of the thousands of things that will ask for your time. The 7s are not on that list. They're the noise that keeps you from hearing the signal.

So the next time someone sends you a perfectly reasonable, genuinely flattering, well-compensated opportunity, and every fiber of your being says "this seems good" — that's your cue to pause. Good is the enemy. Not of perfect. Of *great*. And great is the only thing worth building a life around.

You don't owe the 7s an explanation. You owe the 10s your calendar.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Chapter 3: The Tao of the Broken Coffee Machine

The office coffee machine broke on a Tuesday, and by Thursday we had built a religion around it.

I should back up. In the early days of the company—before the funding, before the press, before anyone's mother understood what we did—there were eleven of us in a converted warehouse with bad heating and a search index that crashed every night around 2 a.m. We had no money for a facilities manager, so when the espresso machine died mid-pull, spraying brown water across the counter, we did what any rational startup does: we ignored it and drank bad drip coffee from a dented carafe.

Except Danny, our third engineer, who refused. Danny had come from a big company where, he claimed, the espresso machine was serviced weekly by a man named Geraldo who wore a tie. Danny took the broken machine personally. He wheeled it—still leaking—to his desk, and over the next three days, between debugging crawler timeouts, he took it apart. He descaled it with vinegar from the kitchen. He replaced a cracked gasket with a piece of silicone tubing from the hardware store. He named the machine "The Oracle" and taped a printout of its internal schematic to the wall above it, annotated in red pen like a war map.

On Thursday morning, The Oracle pulled a shot. It was, objectively, a terrible shot—bitter, thin, slightly metallic. But Danny carried it around the office like a newborn, and one by one, people started lining up. Someone brought in a bag of beans. Someone else wrote a shell script that posted the machine's status to IRC. By Friday, there was a sign-up sheet, a small library of mugs, and a rule—enforced by nobody and obeyed by everyone—that whoever pulled the last shot ground beans for the next person.

I've thought about that coffee machine for years, because it taught me something about culture that no management book ever did.

Culture isn't what you write on the wall. It's what someone fixes when no one asks them to.

We never had a values document in those days. What we had was Danny, elbow-deep in a leaking espresso machine at 11 p.m., and a group of people who noticed and joined in. The Oracle became the office's social center, its status board, its small daily ritual. New hires learned within a week that you didn't just take coffee—you left the machine better than you found it. That norm, silly as it sounds, bled into everything. People started fixing things nobody owned: the flaky deploy script, the onboarding doc, the broken chair. Nobody assigned it. It just became who we were.

The practical lesson, and I'll be blunt about it because I wish someone had been blunt with me: you cannot install culture, but you can protect it. Founders spend enormous energy on mission statements and offsites, and almost none on noticing what's already growing in the corners. The Oracle wasn't in any plan. It emerged because we left enough slack in the system—unstructured time, physical proximity, no one policing how people spent their breaks—for it to happen. The moment you optimize all the slack away, you optimize away the Danny moments too.

The corollary is darker: the norms that form in the cracks can be bad ones just as easily. A snarky IRC channel becomes a hazing ritual. A "we'll fix it later" shortcut becomes a permanent culture of debt. Culture forms whether you tend it or not—your only choice is whether you're paying attention.

We eventually got real funding and a real espresso machine, serviced by a real company. It made better coffee. Nobody loved it. The Oracle sat in a corner, unplugged, until a facilities contractor threw it out during an office move. Danny rescued the schematic from the wall and framed it. It hung in every office we ever had after that, a red-pen monument to the idea that the smallest unasked-for act of care is worth more than any values slide you'll ever build.

If you're in the early days now, look around your office. Find the broken thing someone fixed without being asked. That's your culture. Protect it, and hire more people like the person who fixed it.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
Your first hundred customers are closer than you think. They are not hiding in expensive ad platforms or waiting to be discovered by a viral post. They are standing right in front of you, in the conversations you already have, in the people you already know, and in the customers you have already served. Word of mouth is the oldest and most reliable growth engine for a small business, and the good news is that you can deliberately engineer it. Here is how to get your first hundred customers by getting people talking.

Start with the people who already trust you. Before you chase strangers, make a list of everyone in your existing network: friends, family, former colleagues, neighbors, suppliers, the person who cuts your hair. You are not asking them to buy from you. You are asking them to think of you when a relevant situation arises. Be specific about who you serve and what problem you solve, because vague requests get vague results. Saying "tell anyone you know who needs a bookkeeper" is forgettable. Saying "if you know a restaurant owner who is drowning in receipts, send them my way" gives people a clear picture they can act on.

Make it easy for people to refer you. A referral dies in the gap between good intentions and effort. Hand people the exact words they need. Give them a short sentence they can forward, a link they can share, or a card they can pass along. The easier you make the act of referring, the more referrals you will receive. Do not assume people know how to describe your business; teach them.

Deliver an experience worth talking about. Word of mouth is not a marketing tactic bolted onto a mediocre product; it is the natural result of exceeding expectations. Look for small moments where you can surprise and delight: a handwritten thank-you note, an unexpected follow-up call, a faster turnaround than promised, a thoughtful extra. People do not talk about satisfactory service. They talk about service that made them feel something. Every customer interaction is a chance to create a story someone will retell.

Ask, directly and often. Most happy customers would gladly refer you if you simply asked. Many small business owners never do. After you have delivered a great result, ask a simple question: "Do you know anyone else who could use this?" Time your ask for the moment of peak satisfaction, right after a win. And do not stop at one ask. Keep the door open over time. A customer who was not ready to refer in month one may refer three people in month six.

Build a simple referral habit into your business. Consider a light incentive, but be careful: rewards can cheapen genuine enthusiasm if they feel like a bribe. Often, a sincere thank-you and recognition go further than a discount. What matters most is that you track where your customers come from. Ask every new customer how they heard about you, and write it down. Within weeks you will see which channels actually produce referrals, and you can invest more energy there.

Finally, make word of mouth visible. Share customer stories with permission. Thank referrers publicly when appropriate. When people see that you appreciate and celebrate the people who spread the word, they are more likely to join in. Your first hundred customers will not arrive all at once, but each one who has a great experience and tells someone else compounds your reach. Start with the people you know, give them something worth talking about, and ask. The conversations are already happening; your job is to give them a reason to include you.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
I used to think my purpose was hiding in a spreadsheet somewhere. Like God had a divine Excel file with my name on it, and if I just prayed hard enough, the cell would light up and say: BECOME A PODCASTER. So I spent years squinting at my life, waiting for the big reveal.

Spoiler alert: it never came like that.

What came instead was a casserole. A friend from church had knee surgery, and I signed up on the meal train because I am a recovering people-pleaser and also I cannot resist a shared Google Doc. I made my mom's chicken enchiladas—the ones with the cream of chicken soup, don't @ me—and dropped them off on a Tuesday. I was in and out in ninety seconds. I figured I'd checked the box.

A week later she called me. Not to thank me for the enchiladas, although she did, but to tell me that on the worst afternoon of her recovery, when she felt invisible and useless and forty-seven kinds of tired, a warm pan of food showed up at her door and reminded her that God hadn't forgotten her.

I hung up the phone and just sat there. I had not solved anyone's problems. I had not written a book or launched a ministry or discovered my spiritual gift. I had heated up a can of soup and some tortillas. And apparently that was enough to crack something open in me.

Here's what I've learned since, and I say it gently because I spent a decade getting this wrong: purpose is rarely a destination. It's a direction. And the direction is almost always toward people.

I used to treat serving like a personality type. Like extroverts with good teeth did it, and the rest of us stayed home and watched Netflix and felt vaguely guilty. But serving isn't a talent. It's a habit. It's the small, unglamorous decision to notice someone and do something.

So here are a few things that have helped me, in no particular order:

1. Start smaller than feels impressive. I used to wait for opportunities that looked good on a resume. Now I look for things that take twenty minutes. A text. A ride. A coffee. A casserole. Jesus talked a lot about cups of cold water, and I think He meant it.

2. Serve the person in front of you, not the person you wish was in front of you. I have absolutely fantasized about serving crowds from a stage. Meanwhile my actual neighbor's trash can had been out for three days. Guess which one God kept nudging me about.

3. Don't wait to feel called. I've never once felt a burning bush about unloading the dishwasher at the church potluck. I just showed up. The feeling usually shows up after the obedience, not before it.

Here's the funny thing about all of this. I set out to be the blesser, and I keep getting blessed. I have cried in parking lots over people I met at a food pantry. I have laughed harder with a ninety-year-old widow than with anyone at a conference. I have found more of myself in giving myself away than in any self-help book I've ever read—and I've read a lot of them, usually in pajamas, usually with a highlighter.

Jesus said whoever loses their life will find it. I used to think that was a riddle. Now I think it's just directions.

So if you're sitting there waiting for lightning to strike, maybe start with the enchiladas. Somebody out there is hungry, and it turns out that's the whole point.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
Most people I meet are exhausted. Not from work, necessarily. From the low-grade ache of wondering if any of it matters. They climb the ladder, hit the number, get the promotion—and the itch is still there. I know, because I scratched that itch for years. I built a career, a reputation, a 401(k) that looked great on paper. And I was miserable in a way I couldn't explain at dinner parties.

Here's what nobody told me: the itch isn't a bug. It's a signal. You were never designed to be the destination of your own life.

Jesus said it plainly in Mark 10:45—the Son of Man didn't come to be served, but to serve. That's not a nice sentiment for a plaque. It's the operating manual. And I ignored it for a solid decade because it sounded like losing.

But watch what happens when you flip the equation. Researchers at the University of Michigan followed folks who did regular volunteer work—just a couple hours a week—and found they were 20 percent less likely to die over a five-year stretch than people who didn't. Twenty percent. That's not a spiritual platitude; that's a survival statistic. Another study out of Stony Brook found that people who gave away money or time to help others reported lower stress and higher life satisfaction than those who spent it on themselves. The givers kept winning. Every time.

You want to know the real kicker? The joy doesn't come from the size of the gift. I've watched a guy with a six-figure salary write a check and feel nothing. I've watched a grandmother on a fixed income hand a cashier twenty bucks for the person behind her and light up like a Christmas tree. The difference isn't the amount. It's the orientation. One is writing a receipt. The other is entering a story.

And here's where I'll get blunt, because somebody needs to hear it: if your Christianity is a private consumer product—your worship playlist, your podcast, your Sunday seat—you're going to stay hungry. You can't mainline sermons forever. Information isn't transformation. At some point you've got to get your hands dirty. Feed somebody. Drive somebody. Sit with somebody in a hospital hallway at 2 a.m. and say nothing useful.

I'm not talking about saving the world. I'm talking about the person in front of you. Mother Teresa had a line I come back to constantly—she said she never looked at the crowds, only at the one. One person. That's the unit of a meaningful life. Not your legacy. Not your platform. The one.

Start smaller than feels impressive. Pick one day a week. Two hours. One person. Do it for ninety days and then try to tell me your life hasn't shifted. I dare you.

Because here's the secret the self-help industry won't sell you: you don't find your purpose by looking inward. You find it by looking outward and moving toward the need. Purpose isn't a feeling you discover. It's a direction you choose. And it almost always points away from your comfort.

You were not saved to sit. You were saved to serve. The chair is comfortable. The chair is also killing you.

title: customer-service business book|building a company culture around delivering happiness
text:
Chapter 7: The Return Policy of the Heart

The most profound lesson I ever learned about customer service came not in a boardroom, but in the fluorescent-lit aisle of a grocery store, watching my four-year-old daughter have a complete and utter meltdown.

It was a Tuesday. The kind of Tuesday where the world feels heavy. I was distracted, mentally rehearsing a difficult conversation I needed to have with a client, and I had made the fatal error of taking my tired, hungry child to the supermarket without a snack. The inevitable happened in the cereal aisle. A box of brightly colored, sugar-frosted loops was denied, and the subsequent sonic boom of her wails echoed through the store.

I felt the hot flush of judgmental stares. I was failing at parenting in public. I scooped her up, abandoned my half-full cart, and made a beeline for the exit, my own frustration bubbling just beneath the surface. As I wrestled her into her car seat, a store employee—a woman I’d barely noticed, maybe in her sixties with kind eyes and a name tag that read ‘Betty’—appeared at my window. I braced myself for a comment, a platitude, or worse, a reprimand.

Instead, she held out a single, perfect chocolate chip cookie from the bakery. “For the road,” she said, her voice a soft, calm hum. Then she looked at my tear-streaked daughter and said, “It’s hard being little, isn’t it? Sometimes you just need a cookie.” She then looked at me, and her eyes held no judgment, only a profound, weary understanding. “And it’s hard being the grown-up, too. You’re doing a good job, Mom. Don’t forget your own snack.”

In that moment, Betty didn’t just deliver a cookie. She delivered grace. She saw a person in distress—not a problem to be managed, but a human to be comforted. She didn’t recite store policy; she embodied a philosophy. She gave me happiness in a moment I felt I deserved none. That single, unscripted act of kindness cost the store maybe fifty cents. Its value to me was immeasurable. It’s a story I’ve told a hundred times. I couldn’t tell you what I was wearing that day, but I can tell you Betty’s name.

This is the heart of building a culture around delivering happiness. It is not a program or a script. It is a mindset that must be cultivated, watered, and protected. It begins with a fundamental shift in perspective: every customer interaction is a moment of truth, and every employee is empowered to be a moment-maker.

How do you build a culture where Bettys flourish? You start by hiring for heart, not just for skill. You can teach someone how to use a register, but you can’t teach them empathy. In your interviews, ask questions that reveal character: “Tell me about a time you went out of your way for someone.” “What does a ‘good day’ at work look like to you?” You are looking for people who find joy in service, who are naturally inclined to see the human first.

Next, you must give your Bettys a license to act. This is the hardest part for many leaders. You must trust your frontline employees to make decisions that deliver happiness. At Zappos, this is legendary—their customer service reps are famously not scripted and are encouraged to do what they feel is right for the customer. This means allowing them to waive a shipping fee, send a surprise upgrade, or, like Betty, offer a cookie. You must build a framework of trust so strong that an employee knows, without a doubt, that an act of kindness will be celebrated, not scrutinized. When you empower your team to solve problems with humanity, you are telling them you trust them. And trust is the ultimate happiness multiplier.

Finally, you must celebrate the stories. Betty’s act wasn’t a line item on a P&L. It was a cultural artifact. Share these stories in team meetings, in company newsletters, in casual conversation. Make heroes of the moment-makers. When you celebrate the small, kind acts, you are codifying your culture. You are drawing a map for everyone else, showing them exactly what “delivering happiness” looks like in action.

A return policy is a rule. A return policy of the heart is a culture. It’s the understanding that every transaction is a chance to create a memory. A good culture is one where a customer feels a sense of belonging and a sense of joy. And it all starts with a single cookie.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
You have a vision in your mind of how something should be. The perfect email, the flawless presentation, the ideal workout routine. It is a beautiful vision, clear and bright. And it is the very thing that is keeping you stuck.

Let’s be honest about what is happening. You are not lazy. Procrastination is rarely about laziness. It is about fear. And for you, the fear is wrapped up in the impossible standard you have set for yourself. You believe that if you cannot do it perfectly, you shouldn't do it at all. This is the trap. The pursuit of the flawless is the enemy of the finished.

Think about the last time you put something off. You told yourself you needed to do more research, to wait for the right mood, to have a clear block of time. But what you were really doing was waiting for the perfect moment when you would be guaranteed to produce a perfect result. That moment does not exist. It is a phantom. You are waiting for a train that is never coming.

The first step to breaking free is to accept a simple, liberating truth: you are going to make mistakes. You are going to produce work that is messy, flawed, and human. And that is not just okay; it is the essential, unavoidable path to creating anything of value. The first draft of anything is supposed to be bad. It is a lump of clay. Your job is not to create a masterpiece in one go. Your job is to show up and start molding the clay.

So, let’s change the game. Stop trying to be a perfectionist and start being a finisher. Give yourself permission to do things badly. This is not an excuse for sloppy work; it is a strategy for getting started. Tell yourself, I am going to write the worst possible first paragraph. I am going to create the ugliest, most basic version of this spreadsheet. I am going to do ten minutes of exercise, and I don't care if it's graceful.

Once you lower the bar to the ground, you can step over it. The goal is not to stay there, but to get moving. Momentum is everything. A bad first draft can be edited. A clumsy workout can be improved. A messy room can be organized. But a project that exists only in your head, in its perfect, unblemished form, is a monument to your fear.

You must learn to separate the act of creation from the act of judgment. When you are writing, you are a creator. Your only job is to get the words on the page. When you are finished, you can become the editor. The editor can be as critical as you like, but the creator must be free. Do not let the critic into the room while the creator is working. They cannot coexist. The critic will paralyze you.

So, your new mantra is this: Done is better than perfect. Progress is better than perfection. Start before you feel ready. The feeling of readiness is not a prerequisite for action; it is a reward for it. You will not feel motivated to start by sitting and waiting. You will feel motivated by the act of starting itself.

Stop looking at the mountain and worrying about how you will climb the entire thing. Just look at the first rock. Your only task is to step onto that first rock. Then find the next one. Do not judge the rock. Do not worry if your foot is placed at the perfect angle. Just step. The path will reveal itself as you move. The confidence you seek will not come from thinking; it will come from doing. It will come from the evidence you collect that proves you can show up for yourself, even imperfectly.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
The first time I tried to "get in shape," I made it exactly four days. Four. I bought the shoes, downloaded the app, told everyone I was becoming a runner, and then my shins filed a formal complaint. Sound familiar? Good. Because I want to tell you about the day I discovered the most powerful secret in habit-building, and it's almost embarrassingly simple: start so small you can't fail.

I mean stupid small. Like, laughably small. One push-up small. One sentence small.

Here's what happened. After my fourth failed attempt at running, I read somewhere that you should just put on your running shoes and walk to the end of the driveway. That's it. That's the whole habit. Some days I'd go back inside. Some days I'd keep walking. But here's the thing — I never once failed, because the bar was on the floor. And eventually, walking to the end of the driveway turned into walking around the block, which turned into jogging, which turned into me owning three pairs of running shoes and a foam roller I still don't fully understand.

The problem with most habit advice is that it's designed for the person you want to be, not the person you are at 6:47 a.m. when your alarm goes off and your brain starts negotiating like a tiny lawyer. "We could do it tomorrow," your brain says. "Tomorrow is basically today but better." And your brain wins, because the habit you designed requires willpower you don't have at that hour.

So stop designing habits for Future You. Design them for Tired, Slightly Grumpy, Currently-On-The-Couch You.

A few things I've learned the hard way:

1. Shrink the habit until it feels ridiculous. Want to read more? Read one page. Want to meditate? Sit for one minute. Your goal isn't the workout — it's the identity. You're not trying to get fit today; you're trying to become someone who shows up.

2. Attach it to something that already happens. I do my one push-up while my coffee brews. The coffee was already happening. I just hitched a ride on it. This is called habit stacking, and it's basically carpooling for behaviors.

3. Never miss twice. You will miss a day. You're human, and humans are magnificent disasters. Missing once is an accident. Missing twice is the start of a new habit called "not doing the thing."

4. Celebrate the tiny win. I used to feel silly checking off "one push-up" on my habit tracker. Then I realized the checkmark was doing more for my brain than the push-up was. Give yourself the little hit of dopamine. You earned it, champ.

The beautiful lie of small habits is that they don't stay small. They grow on their own, like sourdough starter or minor clutter. The one push-up becomes five becomes a real workout, and you never once had to white-knuckle your way through a heroic life overhaul.

So here's my challenge, and I promise it takes less time than reading this page: pick one habit you want. Shrink it by 90%. Do that version today. Tomorrow, do it again. That's it. No app required. No shin splints. Just you, being slightly less ambitious and way more consistent — which, it turns out, is the whole game.

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Chapter 7: The Conversation You're Not Having

Let me tell you about my friend Danny. Danny is smart, hardworking, and underpaid. I know this because Danny told me over beers one night, right after telling me he'd just closed the biggest deal of his career. "They should be paying me more," he said. "Are they?" I asked. "Well, no, but they know what I'm worth." Do they, Danny? Do they really?

Here's the uncomfortable truth I've watched play out over and over: most people never ask for a raise. Not once. They wait. They hope. They drop hints. They convince themselves that good work speaks for itself, that management will notice, that the universe rewards quiet excellence. It doesn't. The universe is busy. Management is busier.

I was Danny for years. I once went three years without a meaningful raise because I assumed my boss would eventually wake up and realize I was underpaid. Spoiler: he never did. When I finally asked, he looked genuinely surprised and said, "Why didn't you say something sooner?" Three years of silent resentment, and the whole fix took twenty minutes.

So why don't we ask? Three reasons, mostly. First, fear. We're terrified the answer will be no, and a no feels like a verdict on our worth as human beings. It isn't. It's a data point. Second, we don't know how. Nobody teaches this stuff. School taught us algebra, not how to negotiate our own compensation. Third, and this is the big one, we assume the system is fair. We assume pay reflects performance. It doesn't. Pay reflects negotiation, timing, budgets, and whether someone happened to be paying attention when you did something impressive.

Here's what actually works. Timing matters more than you think. Ask after a win, not during a budget freeze, not right after a layoff. Do your homework: know what people in your role, in your city, in your industry actually make. Sites like Glassdoor and Levels exist for a reason. Then make the ask concrete. Don't say "I feel I deserve more." Say "Based on my results and market data, I'm looking for a bump to X." Bring receipts. That report you saved the company, the client you landed, the process you fixed. Numbers, not feelings.

And here's the part nobody tells you: be ready to hear no, and have a follow-up ready. "What would need to happen for us to revisit this in six months?" That single question turns a rejection into a plan. I've used it. It works.

The worst outcome of asking is usually a no. The worst outcome of not asking is years of quiet resentment and thousands of dollars you'll never get back. Danny finally asked. He got a raise, an apology, and a new title. His only regret was waiting so long.

Ask. The worst they can say is no. The worst you can do is never find out.
